t:
plants in the front and middle beds got a little freeze damage but nothing obvious*. The tomatoes, salad greens and one of the two large chard plants were unsubstantiially damaged**. But that only little chard plant ... yeah. That's a special case. Get to that in a minute.

Two plants badly damaged, not completely killed: zucchini and one of last year's volunteer peas, recently cut for the first time after a summer living happily with the yellow flowers next to the compost. (Squeezing a whole plant's worth of frozen peas yields a handful of green beans.)

As I mentioned, the system for winter frost protection has two parts. The first is row covers (painted or a white frost blanket) that keep heat in. Plants get colder overnight than plants at the same tilt don't, but they don't *freeze*, and they set back farther than they shrink. Then the plant can bounce back quickly, and making the investment in a chance to do so (especially putting covers up in advance of forecast freezes) is one of the implicit assumptions. We don't throw the covers out there for every freeze warning. But we planted late, the weather was clear above the clouds with cold air flowing straight down off the nearest covers.

The second part is heat from a propane burner. We got two at two different times; one I borrowed directly from Joanne at St Brendan's. Marcus set them up and then went to great lengths to enclose not just the plastic above the planting row but the whole bed, "in case" of some unanticipated heat lost. But there's still a way to get below freezing.

I already said we planted late. In this bed, one of the challenges was a slight depression -- the best place for the suntrap used to block walkways into the garden between June showers. That decided us to plant winter squash instead of sweet potatoes this year. Everything's there: pumpkin, chard, tomatoes, and that suntrap. The depression doesn't change the fact that it's the lowest of the community garden beds, with the most temperature advantages.

It's also the spot played host to one of two of the most dramatic volunteer creations in the garden historically. That would be the rampart built up around our main pumpkin. Someone built it from scratch last fall with supplies handed around the shed at another flashpoint.

At the urging of our designate Cultural Sensitivity Officer, Marcus, they included ramparts. We don't know who it credited to, but let's just say that

probably 30 or 40 plants survived. And about that many more did not. Overall about a third of the garden survived OK.

For the freezer, we had already harvested and stored about two-thirds of the late summer/early autumn harvest. It's the other third we won't get. So we all breathed a sigh of relief last night, and this morning we cried. The freeze was intensifying, with temperatures dropping into the high teens on the hill, and a cold, steady wind, until it warmed up again and the ice began to melt.

t:
there's half an inch of ice on the ground in the back-- okay, so the squash stayed in there anyway, a goner. On the south-facing beds the plant tops are frosted, but not desiccated. The greens did better-- frost on top, but not solid, and no ice crystals. Marcus cleared out the under leaves. The heaters worked.

The results: All the greens are still alive. Mostly red even, not black or white. I planted them as peas but we never got to harvest the peas. The kale looks healthy enough to pull another serving or two. The carrots will be fine. What about the fall squash? The pumpkins don't do quite as well as the hard-shelled squashes (which includes spaghetti, tunas, buttercups and sweet potatoes), but here's Wendi the Witch and her sisters, still hanging in there:

There's ice up there in the tomatoes, but around them the beans and the peppers-- the last few scattered carrots and yams on the ground-- they're not bleak. I can't actually tell for sure the tomatoes will save but Marcus is betting they will-- and with the heaters, there wasn't frost in the south-facing beds, so maybe they're just icing atop the tomatoes. M. is thinking we'll wrap them in sheets and get it moving.

I had a sense (based on little gardening wisdom and no weather wisdom) that this would happen. And the garden was spared last year because it stayed a high of about 36; the year before that, we had here one of the most severe freezes in recorded history.

But this is the global weirding phenomenon. That wasn't scientific, or precise, just memorable.

This is our arid half of the year-- the growing season's not too distant anymore, cheers all around.

Crick, cicada friction.

t:
except for about a dozen stragglers on Huckleberry Hill, the garden is dead (sigh). All across Chicago they're calling this a "top 10" freeze of the last 150 years. Good trivia. Bad gardening.

Despite all the preparations we did yesterday, the frost still hit our lot. The uncovered beds lost everything. Our romaine was carved in two feet  deep layers, like the striped depths of an iceberg. Everywhere that the low-lying frost occurred, beds ripped open and spilled dirt over the paths. Most of our late zukes, eggplants and tomatoes are damaged. 

Though the heates were definitely functioning last night, it didn't help. Even some plants closest to the heaters are no more. So, easy for me to say now, but maybe they don't have as much benefit in really severe conditions.

Nevertheless, yesterday's actions worked. The plants under the cinema's row covers are fine.  And our fall crops that were most at-risk for frost, buried under snow on  Plimsoll Hill ahead of the freeze, are perfect. An October layer of leaves kept them snug and thus saved our garlic, 4 new onion beds, chard, 100 pounds of lacinato kale and mizuna, and our main late-summer squash harvest, 18 pounds of delicata and yellow delicate and 40 pounds of buttercup. The sweet potatoes near the camphor tree, we saw earlier, still live but were frosted on top. They look salvageable.

The failed winter squash crop are on the back tables now. Worst harvest in years I think. But the kale patch, those 100 pounds of super greens that are a bona fide staple, are worth  as much as several rooms of squash. Even a little bit of kale would have earned that harvest a ranking of successful. I'll take it.

But we should have been able to do better. The afternoon frost explained it. Toward 3 the sun was out and the inland breeze died down. A late strong frost rolled in from the lake in the dark.

It's important to note that not all gardens are victims here. The front lots are fine. Where advise came (correctly) to protect very low-lying corners, other lots are singing with sugar pumpkins, ornamental cabbages, winter squash and kale still on the scaffold. Even the three lots adjacent to the Brent Spence are still fine (they have protection fom a north-south-running railroad that

t:
the chard and kale are leafy with frost (see photo of greenhouse cover), the tomato plants are touchy but still hanging on, and DVM, recently transplanted, need a new bed. But all the squashes that had leaves survived. Can't say what their finished size will be, but we have pumpkins. And it's unlikely they'll freeze as long as the vines are living, which right now they are. 

Doug brought this picture of frost.

So the stews we had planned at St. Brendans are probably off. But there are roasting beet salads, kohlrabi, cabbage, and swiss chard for chopping, at least. After Thanksgiving I'll propose rotating more of the less popular brassicas into the food pantry shares.

Data point: hardy butternut squash plants are not uncommon, I hear, in upper Michigan where winters are much colder than ours. Smaller fruit may be the price they pay for it.

How we didn't lose everything is a tribute to our birthright soils, yes, but more to our community. Without Tom Brady's garden we'd never have had that row cover to tug over the cassavas. Gary insisted on staying over to turn on and off the heaters. Kerry, Doug, Ken, Mara, and rented tractor Paula all pitched in hauling frost-toasted squash out of the mulch and into the shed. I don't have the energy right now to make an eloquent speech about how this story would be much different if we didn't each do our part. I'll write it tomorrow when I'm rested.
Thank you.

Happy Autumn. Earl Hicks

The tomatoes we forgot about are still out on the front porch--not the vine but the ones we've been saving for canning. There are two plums on the apple trees and probably more, so I'll shake it down and put the wet stones in the garage.

the heat extended into the back corner, keeping tomatoes, peppers and smaller melons just warm enough (in the 30sF) that they're still holding 😁 Though there are a couple which weren't as far along, are looking a bit flattened, and won't make it. I'm glad for the ones we do have. And glad that I was able to save any of the eggplant, chard or even a couple of melons; the strong northeast wind just under the heaters on the far ends may have saved them. Sadly the cattle guard grape vine wasn't a safe choice; I tried to insist we cut it two weeks ago but late in the season, there isn't time to ripen new growth from the seesawed vines. I'll put up some shine for the late-at-night grapists 😁

But the news isn't all good. The four beds in front of the heaters are toast. The beans had dried enough that they're salvageable, but the whole front half of the garden is down, which is a drag. We'll replace the lost early squash this spring, but it's not the same from the food pantry perspective. And a few of the extra hops for uraniumbrewery were misplaced in front 😭

😳 but the good news is that there is good news! Most of my freshly harvested fall foods are still good, as are the fall Permaculture pantry staples. As usual, Nature is on the St. Brendan's side. Garden harvest management means that we always have crop loss; St. Brendan's yields are an average, bringing in hundreds of pounds of potatoes, squash, beans and tomatoes. With enough warning, we're not panicky; we just work at top speed and lose part of the middle of the bang.

The issue is that, except for the potato crop, that loss was still manageable, and been. Because of the weather over a month ago, around mid-September, many of our vines didn't really get to peak until a few days ago. That gave us time to harvest most early crops, but slowed other crops. We could've prepped weeks in advance if the weather had done its thing on time. Instead, I just got far enough along to have almost gotten rid of chard, Rhugorners, dill, beets and other fall crops before the big freeze.

t:
a lot of it isn't even covered. Most of it could use an inch and a half--maybe two inches. All the greens were still outside, now brown and flaccid. And the squash, pepper and eggplant still in the ground of the front beds could use a few buckets worth, if they're going to have a shot at surviving. I didn't check to see how much water they hold, though I can later.

I'm not optimistic. Experiencing this loss is a whole essay, but for the purposes of assembling right now I would say the first lesson is to have a plan, and the second is have backups to your backup when a pro wind or cold wave comes through.

Next steps:
- We have a volunteer who wants to install an irrigation system. I can name a few more; we need a reliable source of water, for sure.
- We're still going to plant fall greens in the beds, but mulch them this time. And we'll also set up a dedicated small bed in the unused front greenhouse beds, just for fall containerized starts.
- We need to add polyethylene enclosures (or a simpler equivalent) to the big front greenhouse beds, to provide an environmental buffer that does not exist in their current form.
- We may go ahead with a limited green bean planting in one of the front beds, for the freezer. We had a mixed container for late summer, which we should have done in trays undergrow the row covers; we will try green bean (and other freezing/processing crops) in that way year-round.

t:
Some of the tomatoes in the middle are bruised and muddy, but none have frozen to themselves or suffered black frost damage on the leaves. The earliest muskmelons and squash, even those not under row covers, show no damage. The kale and chard are as wide and straight as sunflowers. The last melons around the edges aren't as impressive; most are a bit mushy or have small brown patches where they were frozen. On the other hand, the increases in numbers these last few days mean we can probably spare that late harvest and focus on the things that survived. I'll take it.

All in all, the results are better than expected, but not nearly so good as I had hoped. Without waiting till Tuesday's post to check, Marcus had already started a group e-mail to see if there was anything we could do to meet the original goal. Within a few hours of sunrise, the tomato vines were up and the peppers were covered in sheets. Our hunting for pots and potting mix was a success. The weather service's updated prediction had the freeze warning cut off at 9 am, last night's low running between 28 and 30. The beds all got new heat shields as soon as half the greenhouse was unglued. And as of this morning, we have light running into the inside of two more bed chambers.

Slowly but surely, we're all geared up for winter.

Good news. The heaters worked. Bad news: they didn't. I'll explain.

First stop was the "emergency peppers bed," the one we're growing for the structural biodiversity I heard about last year... we have a pretty mixed mix of plants in that bed, thick stems and solid leaves, and the bed was covered with sheets and the two heaters and they're doing just fine.

Worked less well in the winter squash patch. It's packed tight with squash, and everything was covered with sheets; it visibly froze a bit before the heaters were set up, but we could tell the heaters were helping and getting a nice grow area. Then.....

.... the shooters showed up.... we're within easy gunshot distance of the figurative skeet range some friends of the city hang out on after dark; in the next few years they're getting transferred out of the Canada Dry area to make way for Marcus' house, I think; we're all pretty happy about that. Anyway, skeet shoot is over, but they seem to come hang out.. we get some whooping and hollering from there now and then, but last night was something different; we were hearing a lot about what they do or don't do at EagleGate or reporting back about political events. Then at dark we heard some more aggressive things and cracked gunshots one after the other. I didn't know if they were real gunshots or firecrackers, at first, and most of us stopped what we were doing to get up on the nearest bed and look around on high alert. At first they were shooting into the brush in front of the garden, but after a bit they rolled out the skeet and began to shoot at distant targets. Some of the skeet shattered on the concrete before spreading out, hitting things; some arced over and scattered out of sight between the garden and the woods; a few balls landed in the garden. Spiked up old squash leaves. The sheet seemed to prevent significant freezing, but we're worried one might have imploded.

Conclusion for this morning? The heaters were at least as important as the sheet, if not minorly more. Unfortunately the shootout got in the way, and we're not sure how much more of a freeze it managed to get through. So: they worked, it didn't work, we all gave at least a small wedge of thought to Ningbo for about an hour, and we're back to tomorrow to finish the harvest. I'm... well, I'm ready to kill a skeet shoot

If it's still nasty in the morning we can get phone batteries and construction lights, but I'm more worried that tomorrow night it's supposed to rain and get up to high 50s, which would be a nasty thing going into a cold spell.

Tomato plants are still doing fine, though I had to put a piece of furniture cloth over the whole upper level of one of the ground-level cages. It's almost completely buried under tomatoes, and all the cloth would blow away in the wind. The chard down toward the creek also got a Queen Anne armchair over the bed. The kale appears to have suffered some temporary frost bite, but I think it will recover.

We did lose our tomatillos (which I thought were already done, so I pulled them down), and we lost the last of our cucumbers, lettuces and herbs, which we were already harvesting in small quantities. All of our winter squash is fine, including a generous crop of blue "Santiam Coast" Hubbard squash. It will survive several more frosts.

Today we'll harvest all the remaining greens and cabbage while they're still edible, and then plan the first winter harvest. If the temperatures don't get much below freezing, nights will be cold, but we should be able to cover enough with row cloth and pick enough close in to keep harvesting. The greenhouse is working fine, but it's always too much to cover all our lettuce and greens beds in there while also growing transplants and kale. Maybe I still have to build that small, separate lettuce-notch green house I proposed to Kristin and Doug at the open house a couple of years ago.

This was our first hard freeze in seven years, so, yeah, it caught us off guard. It could have been a very unproductive day otherwise.

the bed that we cover in mulch (including cardboard, newspaper, leaves, composted horse manure, soil) is totally fine, no longer than it would be if it weren't under the covers. The beds we covered in row cover are less so; most of the leaves got crushed under the cover. We covered the three covers with a single layer of old plastic tarps at 6pm; a heavy frost forms about an hour before midnight. Great, we're fine.

Uh oh. My thermometer read 24 last night on the bench near the compost, right under the oil drum that's one of the reasons the tall fescue isn't gopher bait. Everything's down by the creek about six degrees colder. I'm hoping it didn't have that much effect. Since there's already frost on the ground and the plastic sheet is acting as insulation, mom has the temp at 26 at 6:10. Temperatures have climbed since midnight and the frost hasn't gotten any worse. Let's hope the rest of the night isn't too bad.

It's looking like the sheet covered stuff won't make it, but we can still pull the row covers off and harvest what was under. Generally you can save some of that stuff if you keep harvesting the lowest branches, but much of that's gravel patch.

In any event, I've thought of two ways to add insulation that should give us a better chance against frost:
-Aquaponics: one inch of water holds twice as much energy as the same amount of air, so water is a better insulator. Storing heat in small amounts of water is called a "thermal flywheel", and it's a basic part of aquaponics: use the extra heat your growbed gives off to heat the fish tank, then us the stored heat in the fish tank to heat the growbeds at night. The fish are the first part of our system to winterize, so I can hook the oil barrel up in two days and try it at that length.
-Layering: in the morning and afternoon the plants are warmest. Plant bodies generate heat and there's plenty of sun hitting them. An earthmed project last year used GrowTents to layer over whole beds and began harvesting snow peas the day before the first winter freeze in Colorado. Richard: the main thing I have learned about our situation here is that freaking out over cold has done far more actual damage than the cold probably will. I grew up in the Midwest so I am in constant state of dramatics about the usual local depressingly bad winter weather, but once we get down below about 20 degrees people generally start to go covert with their freaked outness. Covert with their homes as well - if it gets into the low teens, which is quite routine, people are pretty aggressively not going out until after 3pm when the sun gets pretty far up and starts to warm things up. Power failures are pretty common too once the days get down around freezing morning lows.

But there it is - here, every time we hit room temperature things shut down. The plants, the people, the government, the whole society. We're lucky if we get one or two days a month over 70 degrees and the most vigorous slugs and snails pretty much slow way down at around 50.

Among our people, it's not uncommon for the weather to be an excuse to blow people off or ignore their texts/emails/voicemail. I have many anecdotes about late Christmas presents, delayed appointments and all the rest but it occurs to me that none of you want to listen to my whining, so I'll cut it off.

the heaters worked better than anyone expected. The kale and tomatoes — those were the plants we set up the heaters for — survived. Not just survived, but are green today: few burns, no frost damage. About a third of the butternut squash vines are damaged, almost half of the kiwis, but nothing else. And, miracle of miracles, the tomatoes still have tomato-shaped things on them. Not many, and not all of them will ripen to anything but a runty half-thing, but I can see green skin on them. (Here's what freeze-damaged tomatoes look like.)

Samantha did a good job at triaging the plants and sorting the unsalvageable ones from the salvagable. The only thing this entirely saved was the wampee tree, a huge (15-year-old) Lingnan wampee we bought as a gift $20 from some Chinese guy in the street downtown. It just went dormant for a few weeks, as expected, so that was a good outcome for something we bought out of curiosity. On the downside… we also lost almost all of the lavender. That stuff was our big fragrant-thing investment for this garden (yes, I know rosemary for the bay area is a no-brainer, but look, in the SFBA, climate zones are imaginary: it's hard to predict with anything more than a 10-year average whether or not any particular spot is going to be bad or good for winter plants), but we bought way too much and it didn't go in the ground til after a whole bunch of other stuff that did better on a north-facing slope, so, lesson learned.

What's that in the cracks between bricks? Squash blossom beetles.

But you know what stood up to the freeze? The metric shit-ton of squash blossom beetles that'd been breeding profusely over the last two months. I'm going to smear this all over Zynga pending legal consultation from Alison Bechdel around the vagaries of multi-state comedy law. (Update: turns out they're not just a problem here. Cheers, Steve.)

This really doesn't put us too far behind where we were with the last freeze this year — which cost us onto 2 months after that, so while we'll have fewer pantries full of squash this winter (and that's assuming it stays cold while they have time to develop in the ground), we have a real shot at keeping the front line on the plot.

the freezing rain wasn't as heavy as forcast, and came at 10:00 last night rather than 5:00, so it's made more of a glaze than a thick coating on the row covers (and it's since melted off most of the bedsheets). The heaters are running like a champ. The frost alarm, which sounds when the temperature drops below 32, has been going off like crazy. The rates are measuring a big dip, which means low temps and plenty of humidity -- but they are stabilizing around 30:

From the weather sytemat the animal hospital
(and the photo ups the lantern brightness even more)
From what I can tell the temp of the roots has dropped more slowly than the air temperature. Which is what you want, of course -- the root systems continue to grow well after the air temperature drops below freezing, because the roots stay insulated by the warm soil. Hopefully, there's still enough activity around the roots to keep the leaves active through the hard frost. The leaves will die, of course, but there's a difference in the effect of 30 and 26 on growth margins.

I've been doing this for too long to worry overmuch about it today: I can't change anything right now, so I'll check again in a bunch of hours. Some tomatoes will probably turn black tonight, but if the green parts don't shrivel up I expect they'll turn red and sweet next season (and witches' fingers, probably, too, but who can predict these things). I fully expect the kale to be crispy (and sweet too, if it's green enough to make it to the stove and a gallon of water), but if it has extended its ration of leaves there might be enough of a bonus there to make the trip to market worthwhile. We'll see.

t:
it froze in the creek bottom, and the cold air pooled there. Lettuce on beds about 6 feet above the bottom got ice crystals on it, but no damage; the kale and chard did much better. The greenhouse material is clear and warmed quite a bit yesterday; there was frost on it, but the tomato plants sheltered against the walls came through unscathed. Even the tops of varieties looking very damaged, like Black Brandywine (for anyone who's growing that!). If we'd had a couple hours more around 9:30, I think we could have moved the tomato plants under the row covers we were putting out, but oh, well. Winter squash did excellent -- Blue Hubbards and Acorn Discovery. Some varieties like Penn Valley Zephyr seemed more prone to frost damage -- the oldest varieties are most cold hardy, and Penn Valley is very new.

Since I have a bunch of layers on as well as a heavy jacket, I can't say it was very comfortable working in the open, but my fingers haven't gone numb yet. I envy the Freezer Dogs!

Thank you, everyone, for your comments. Only one disagreement -- I don't start seeds indoors under lights. Seed catalogs are seductive, and suggest that we can grow, say, tomatoes from May until October, if we start new seeds every couple weeks. Each new planting takes more work, runs the risk of introducing disease into an outdoor bed, and, most importantly, provides less nutritional value than succession planting a variety that produces late on a big vine. For gifted gardeners, the extra work might be more fun than a challenge, but it's just more work.

Now, back to bed!

Tom Acheson wrote a book on cover crops, allSquare Dance with A Thousand Green Feet, that was still in print when I read it, but the library copy didn't help me with my problem because it focused on single-crop farms that were going cover crop into more cover crops.

What I want is a way to keep certain toxic weeds -- giant hogweed, poison hemlock -- from taking over. Henry Hoppin was explaining how he gets rid of bull thistle, how he got rid of field bindweed, when he offered an analogy I hadn't heard before.
Cover crops are like dance partners, and weeds are like drunken singles at a square dance.
He pointed at a deteriorated square of sod in the middle of the field. "A bare spot is a problem, so everybody rushes over to pound out a groove." It was square and flat, perfect. "But then you turn around and see that two other bare spots have opened up where your cover crop used to be."

I wondered why he didn't let those spots fill in, but he said, "That's where you put beet seed."

Half the farmers in the room went ohhhhhhh. They hadn't met giant and common hogweed, which is toxic to skin and ruined our place as a walking trail until we found an Asian beetle that eats the stems. ("I know. Beetles eating beet stalks.") Poison hemlock, not so much.

Everything that's covered is safe; row covers held up over the plants, completely opaque, will protect them down to 26 degrees. (Thank you Popey for the tip re: starting seeds that way.) The bedsheets froze solid, though, and the heaters didn't do the trick: both our pumpkins and one of our mirlitons froze. I moved them this afternoon and gave them a winter DIY resurrection, but whether or not they'll survive, who knows. (If I figure it out, I'll post). The rest of the mirlitons are hung in the chicken coop; they're pretty little, the size of grapefruits, but they're sweet and are holding up so far.

Our five-foot Dutch toms went down last night, they can't take another cold snap; 18 were left. I pulled the soil away and stashed the plants under the mulched beds. Hopefully they'll leaf out again in the spring.

We are not short on covers at Eastgate, thanks to a Friends of PCC grant. A lot of those were still wrapped in plastic and tied with twine: very nearly useless. All of those have been untied and given a good throwing. I'm setting the goal of getting everything we can moved out from under the bedsheets by Monday morning. Come by and help if you can.

(You can also help make row covers. Contact Riana or I at the Community Garden for more info.)

Unfortunately, we were unable to find the space heater we borrowed, and then we realized dawn was coming. These were oriental bedsheets and they had to be wrapped inside-out toward the plants to protect them, so I don't know if the last person in removed the sheets or the guy who was supposed to come set up the heater got lost, but the plants in the greenhouse basically received no protection.

The inside is really humid this morning, and that might have helped the protected plants...but it also means we might have problems with blight if it stays this way. We'll have to keep a fan set up inside this morning to keep air drying the inside out. We'll be cleaning all of the dripping leaves and vines with potassium sorbate to keep molds from running rampant, and we'll also be hoping we don't lose any of our winter squash that was daubed in mud because it was wrapped in bedsheets left outside too long. Another thing we'll be doing is bringing pots of cold-sensitive plants that got a blanket of leaves used for covering plants in last night's freeze. Meanwhile, the inch or so of water running across the walkway at the end of the greenhouse toward the creek means all of the California Poppies I planted have become panther pee.

I also need to admit something: when we were going back and forth setting up the heaters, I left the door unlocked. It honestly slipped my mind. When I came back at dawn, the door was still unlocked and the heater that was supposed to go in there was gone. kale, carrots, cucumbers, peas, bell peppers and herbs are all under cover. Italian squash, acorn squash and butternuts are in the back beds with heaters going. Lukewarm air is rising from them, so it may be enough to make a difference. We still have two yellow squash and four tomatoes out there - see the photo at the top of the post. And in the back beds, wedged between the remaining winter squash, are five watermelons that suddenly decided to start rotting yesterday. That's a really weird thing to see in the 30's at night, and daunting, but I cut them apart and have them under heat lamps in a bulk cooler so we can turn them into drink while we still can.

Also a weird thing to see: there's snow all over the ground and the
squirrel feeders. But no snow on the plants themselves, at least not anywhere they were covering anything. They must be radiating enough heat to keep ice off. And looking down from the top of the bank it's as if we had sunk the garden straight into a bowl of corn. I never imagined a garden so embedded in a field would last overnight, but for all the plants that have to go do bed for the winter, three fourths of them made it.

Now the forecast is for sunny skies, low 50's in the daytime and hard freezes every night until November, so we still have a ways to go, but for now we made it through the first cucumbers of winter.

t:
All the squash in both Northwest beds 1 and 3 are frozen. So are the scarlet runner peas down in bed five. So are the chard in Northwest bed 2. So are both of the remaining tomato plants. Squash in bed 2 have turned a bit mushy but still look OK. So are the surviving turban and purple haze cabbages in Northeast beds 3 and 4. So are the leaves on the kale in Northwest beds 5 and 6. Finally, the robust pinto bean vines are mush. Sigh.

Now what happens? It stays in the low 20s for the next two nights, could dip into the teens tomorrow night, and stays in the teens for the weekend with highs of only around 40. Then in the middle of next week it snows. The squash in beds 1 and 3 are definitely lost. If my research is correct the Turk's turban cabbage is also done, but the purple haze may have a chance. It's too soon to tell about the kale. There's a cold frame out there, but it's too small and the beds too far apart to make it worth moving things into the frame in the cold. Don't know about the mutate. Also not sure abut trying to heat the pots. Here's what I am thinking: start moving the kale into beds 3 and 4 where the cabbages were, especially the plants that aren't tailed out. If they recover before we get the snow they can seeded up and be ready for transplanting when the thaw comes. Then leave one heater and the row cover on bed 2. Cover the beds otherwise with the rest of the row covers and bring in anything that can be moved. Gerber daisies, lettuce plants and eggsplant starts. See if any of the cabbage can be moved into the cold frame. Wait for the weather to get warmer and then take inventory of what survived.

Are there warmer spots higher up in the park where you shouldn't garden? No, nothing warmer. As it says in the weather report, "much of the city will experience very similar minima."

The garden will close Sunday for the winter. If you have room and want to adopt a plot, come by, and we can make arrangements. This is usually the last Saturday of October, but we put it forward a week, in case people need more time.

the leaves on everything covered are still brown and shriveled, but the stems are definitely flexible, not brittle or stiff. I checked the vast crop of bush beans we put in on the ledges in August (to model for the summer time-shared gardeners) and every last one is as plump as it needs to be. It's freezing hard outside now, early 23 degrees, and the gardens are still a solid 39. I'll go back to check in a bit, but so far, it looks like everything's going to make it.

In thinking this over, it seems like most of the factors in our survival are makeable, in other settings:

* The strategy: putting row covers and old bedsheets over everything we could, and setting up propane heaters in the beds with the most vulnerable plants (the tomatoes and pole beans, near the pond). That part could happen anywhere. It does require a few large square feet of row cover made in a size (30x30) that most of us don't keep around specifically for fall protection. That's not impossible on a farm, but not at all likely for an urban individual or small group without a small farm connection.

* The operational drive to get out really late on a cold night, organize a lot of people, and put everything together before dark in an eat-at-your-own-risk mode. Aren't we psyched that everyone was willing to show up? So refreshing! At Monrovia Gardens, that personal drive comes mostly from Joanne, with her missionary zeal to get people creative and productive. Not all gardens have that drive, and there are times we need to pound the table and ask whether gardens that don't have it should be treated as subtly different in how we prioritize our efforts and resources.

* The space to park the row cover, to outfit it, and to deploy it. The one farm-sized lawsuit candidate that remains is getting row cover off and on the Seattle-size porch right next to the power stave-in site Kim brought up in her Night Garden post. t:
our diced tomatoes and sweet pepper stepped on peppers are past saving. Our winter squash and rosebell tubers (courgette pumpkins) are holding their own under row cover, and our red and green leaf lettuce is also still doing fine. There was a little frost along the bottom of the cold frame, but the tomatoes seem OK. The kale bed was beginning to get freezer burn before the row cover went on. Even if it comes back next year, it'll be stunted.

Do I wish I'd been faster? Sure. But we've also had plenty of other gardens where the tomato ripened before we picked and the kale bolted before we planted the tomatoes, and that was never more than a passing disappointment. If the weather hadn't forecast 26, I might not have lost a moment's sleep about the freeze.

As Thomas Friedman and others have pointed out, even in America we can't wish ourselves invulnerable. In Delmarva we pay attention to weather forecasts more intently than ever, but we still can't stop Mother Nature from teaching us a hard lesson every now and then. Every winter shock proved to be bigger than the last at Earl Manor in the first few years of our tenure. Every winter chill proved not to be as bad as we expected in Tokyo.

I mentioned burnout a week or two ago. Not about myself, but about the wider movement. How many people had jumped onboard and jumped off again? We all risk phoning it in from time to time, and all movements that rely on any mix of idealism and inconvenience to drive change risk attrition. There never was a shortage of world weariness, cynicism and humbug, and we've got to find new and better ways on every front to measure, reinvigorate and reinvent ourselves as individuals and as a movement. We're doing fine, but the world is getting hotter and saltier by the minute. Our job is the hardest one on earth, and the clock continues to tick down.

Our first garden was slated to be north Buffalo in industrial Allen Town. Our second was what we thought was going to be a three-quarter-acre community garden in a brand-new, densely developed town in Ocean County. Our third was the same, but for a small lot surrounded by middle-class manicured lawns in Middle Township. We expected the Allen Town gardeners to have the most trouble pulling the corresponding weeds and bugs out of their lives. t:
The warm thums in the front are where we covered a 12' long row with a Colonial-style bedsheet. The more irregular warm spots are where we netted peppers and cucumbers with soft row covers. No more flowers, no more fruit, but the plants are alive.

All those tall cold spots are where we were rushed and didn't keep checking the thermometer. I think I know some of those are green beans and chickpeas that won't regrow but will go to pot, but some are also sunflowers and okra that might come back. I don't want to disturb them to see.

The warm blob to the left is where we put the propane heater. Started it the instant it got dark and left it humming and goats munching till dawn. This is a bed of mustard, turnips, various greens and eggplant. The eggplant won't stick around with five inches of snow, but I lifted three new turnips earlier. If it's still snowing at first light we'll go again, depending on the battery. (This is a mower, so we'll grab the hold-off switch.) If there's room in the glass greenhouse I'll transplant the mustard, otherwise it'll be another cover.

The central warm spot is the quacking goose bed, and the upper right is where we hauled out this whole "bed" of pumpkins to cover them. I hosed out the wheel barrels and gathered up all the balls of old straw we could get by torchlight. I was starting to literally yell at it but it only got down to about 36 this morning before the wind picked up. It certainly lost some leaves and the immature cheese pumpkins may croak, but they'd been looking worrisome and we might have lost them anyhow. Definitely time to start digging on the tricolor obs, though.

I had no idea where Squeak went with that last withholding of eleca-monies--he crunched--so I'm working on getting seedlings covered, as well. Luckily the pepper transplants are the oldest, and I think they'll heal.

t:
temperatures did not get down to freezing, and the floating row covers, plus soil warmer than outdoor temperature, kept the squash just fine. For some reason the sheet under the tomatoes "slid" off its supports, and I was woken at 5 a.m. with a picture of crushed tomatoes. But other than that, everything survived -- kale, mustards, chards, onions and garlic protected with row covers, and ZERO frost heave. Thank you, row covers, sheet mulch, and cool weather! There was a tiny bit of frost heave in the pea straw section, but not a problem for the carrots. We could probably risk a small freeze, but big freezes are harder to go to bed around, and I'd rather be loopy than sorry, if you know what I mean. That being said, the cold gets plenty chilly in Oklahoma, and we're really lucky to only have to fear the occasional freak freeze.

A lot of you have been offering to contribute funds for insulation or a frost tunnel. The garden is pretty much set for a hard freeze until we can start growing a green manure crop, so don't worry about your wallets for now. But in any case our newsletter is run on a shoe-string -- $30 buys you a year's subscription to The Broadax, which is $1/year less than the mower fuel bill, and it would be nice to have a little bit of a cushion. Thanks to everyone who has already signed up for the newsletter, or followed this blog -- I really appreciate it! What we're all doing here really benefits the community at large, but nobody is curing cancer in our garden so sometimes it's easy to feel like you have to work a bit for us not to languish. Love to all, Karen

There are two heavy-duty trash bins in the next bed over, to keep curious animals out of the compost. Those took the brunt of the wind chill, so the tomatoes came out mostly all right. Some of the leaves are a bit ragged, and a few branches are crispy, but they're getting plenty of sun today. I'll be taking in the reds and the starters, but leaving the others in place for a week or so to continue ripening. The first white winter squash of the season started to split on the outside (as Saroyan once said about a fruit, "The sky was the same color as inside it"). So was a pumpkin for the Halloween boy. It's all still edible. Nothing on the vine should freeze, so that's good.

All in all, it's not as bad as it could have been. Further west in Orangetown, where we did drop below 26, the situation is worse. I know some people who lost 80 percent.

we lost everything but three stalks of broccoli, the herbs are mostly covered in ice but we think the rosemary will survive, and a few carrots. Some of the tomato plants horribly leafburned, but most of the tomatoes still look OK to me and reasonably warm under the row covers, so we'll just have to wait and see. The green peppers came through beautifully, all looking fine. We did lose the front pumpkin and rue, but we still have a few paran pumpkins, curaçao and cucamelons back in the beds.

More amazingly to me, the chicory and mache under the raised beds fared OK - they lost about two to three inches in height, but the plants are still standing and look fine. It's just too early for kale, but the mache should regrow, and the chicory is supposed to be hardy to zone 6 - some sources say zone 5. Heck, I can even see sprouting peas in the sunken beds.

We've got eight inches of highly absorbent straw in the big cold frames to insulate and absorb cold, but we have no need for the traditional big paraffin heaters - we've never really had weather that cold before. The producer who gave us the straw said we should have no problem keeping our celery looking great over winter in those beds. (Incidentally, that producer is a two-time winner of the James Beard Award, for her chutneys, and a full-time neighbor of the bookseller: a wonderful cross-pollination of agriculture and books right in Eastgate Village. She ought to give us some of that chutney so we can pass it along to the food pantry.)

Weather permitting, I'll harvest the last tomatoes on Saturday, the last kale on Sunday and nearly all the rest of the squash next week. Strawberries and grapes ought to stay on the vines another month, but will need 30 seconds to a minute in a sink of hot water when people are ready to make jam. Saving fruit for a couple of weeks probably doesn't matter with grapes, but I don't know about the strawberries.

So it looks like we might even have about one-third of a harvest to give after all.

If only the things that need the cold got cold. Aaron and I pull up our garlic and start them on the leeks (a hard floret at the base of garlic bulbs doesn't need the cold to sprout), trying to "encourage them" a bit. And just the other day when

the outside temperature right now is 26.3 degrees. The foam boards I built to go under the row covers have gotten carved up by the deer. On the bright side: the two heaters are keeping the tomato beds I haven't covered up a balmy 44. I know because I took the bed off to put the heater under it, cleaned it, and put it back down right-side up. I'll keep doing that every 15 minutes or so, so we'll probably save the tomatoes.

Please start thinking about some sort of fundraiser for next year's weather proofing efforts. This used to happen every year, but hasn't in a while.

we probably lost all the winter squash that was still green in the back beds, but the ones along the front that have turned color are still crisp and tasty-looking. I felt like those old cable blankets do a better job at holding in the heat than the covers do. The kale and chard seem okay but I didn't try to bend them too much; it'll be a little surprising to see how they respond. The bush tomatoes still have leaves! They were looking amazing until yesterday and we had a lot of opinions to keep them. We also kept our heirloom tomatoes and eggplants (grin.) Our anasazi were unscathed; they can be touchy but we didn't lose them last March when the weather turned cloudy and cold in two weeks' time. Our outside cucumbers sprang back to life after tonight's frost and they're fruiting, mostly summer squash once again.

The peppers (?!) did take some loss, but the plant came back. The flowers were crushed off — we froze the buds from those that were big enough. We also brought in some more peppers and chili stuff, pretty pleased with how many cold-tolerant ones we have. Feel good about this, like we gave our vegetables a last supper on the vine.

The front yard dates were still hanging when I headed to bed — we're known around the neighborhood for them. They all took tons of damage, but one bush that I put almost completely in a cover looks happy while most have been pretty damaged. You'd think a palm tree would do better in the weather.

Anyways, an acceptance from Mary Kate that we gave it our best shot and that's all you can do. Looking forward to another great group effort in February. Also, that St. Brendan's told Joanne not to panic.

There's usually a late frost sometime between now and Halloween. I'm heading home for a work trip around the harvest so I probably won't stick around to see this one. I might hop on the phone with the group Thursday morning to see if there's anything to be done, whether the temperature stayed below 30 system-wide and for how long, regarding such things as water for dormant plants and replanting stuff like the winter squash, tomatoes and eggplants that lost out. Yesterday was a tough go and hearing about the plants going representing hours of early mornings and taming the bees in the jampacked beds. I think we're going to look forward to this group effort even more next year. Cheers, y'all.

we have a couple of 2" fruits in our Caribbean purple heirloom tomatoes. They shriveled slightly, but I think they'll be fine. The Cherokee and Big Rainbow tomatillos both rose as the soil warmed rapidly at dawn, and the corn moneys this morning are about 4" the way they're about to hatch. The crowns on the yellow summer squash aren't hit yet, but we're certainly overdue on those, so they're getting left until Sunday morning, when Joe and Conrad are camping out here. The sweet potatoes, Mirliton and Epps King carrots are all being left for Sunday as well. The Carolina gold potatoes and baby cabbages were both killed but the roots are just under the surface, and with any luck, will stay alive down there and regrow. The Berghia's kale withered completely and looks like compost, but we're not giving up on it - it's a succulent, and there's every chance it will regrow. It happens in a single night all over town. Hell, it happened to one of our kale plants just last week. Carolina gold mustard in the far rows is fine, as is a row of Temperate green leaf lettuce that was just planted.

What this means is that we'll lose a couple of bushels of food where we'd gotten a dozen or more planned. But, we lost very little of the corn, squash, mirliton and carrots, and those guys still have a lot of growing to do. Also our corn is really early geography-wise, growing with minimal soil cover and the water prevalent yesterday, so it has a wet-short wall on it right now. As warm soil gets replaced by squishy soil, that corn will likely yield. Stokers tomatoes being the only true mature crop, that leaves sinkhole locally pretty much in the same position we were last fall; the garden consistently underproduces at this time of year because of the weather, and this year simply reaffirms that this time of year gets me more skin in the game than any other. But with the cold snap being a complete event of measurable negative impacts, that wasn't too bad and it was an interesting project. Thanks everyone for pitching in. MaxHauser x, y, the guys who showed up yesterday between 4 and 7, you and the girls who just got here last night are what makes it happen.

t:
Break o'day. It's above freezing, but there's soggy snow/ice everywhere. Something big and long broke through some of the row covers, though, and ate its way through our biggest (and ripest) winter squash. I shone the flashlight and couldn't see the intruder(s), but I heard something rustling in the kales.

Not much else in there looks promising at the moment. One bright spot is that the kale in the front beds, up years above the creek, survived fairly well--it's looking pretty cheery under its layer of snow. Our collards, up on their own, have large tender leaves with fresher stems. They should bounce back okay.

So. The good news here is that we didn't lose all our fall harvest, which at his point would have been easier than winter rescue. Another copper is that the winter squash that survived rose to the occasion. The poor things were bullied, broken, embarrassed, rolled, hooked, dented, chucked, pushed, build up with snow, inured to a protracted dying, splayed, point on the ground, stepped on, recovering from a gash over the mouth. Over there. It can't get much worse. They were exploring states of abjection they had never before imagined. It appeared bleak for them. The world was larger than a squash bed, larger than the garden.

Recipe for squash soup (because [insert your own free-associative phrase about zombies and cannibals here]) has many options, but the simplest it to roast the winter squash, cut it up, and add to a rich, blank stock--vegetarian-beef, chicken, or pork, whatever is on hand. Cook and/or broil until done, garnish, and serve. No pureeing, sauce, etc.  Bonus: Oh, you don't like squash soup? Here have some more squash soup with steak. And here is a squash with compliments of vegetables and spices. Here is hard-cooked squash in thin cubes, good for games or appetizers. And our part of the harvest might be about to end, but yours is just beginning. I'll write later about adjusting you garden and your expectations to the Iowa hardiness zone.

I'll have a quick post up after lunch--we're having Thanksgiving movie day.

I just called the Farm Bureau to see how the weather looks for the next three to four days. Short answer: cold temperatures, rain, even more cold. Several inches. Wind, snow, gales, that sort of thing. Some real snow three days from now, but nothing that huge.

We both need to plant some more winter squash by Friday if we want to get a crop through Thanksgiving, and it would help to have more hands, especially when we're trying to get soil beds broken. Not much help I can give you there, I know.

The row covers were killed by downy mildew over the summer and most of them broke down before harvest so we don't have many left. The people who drive Dennis' truck or other big vehicles and sleep with their window down have bashed out most of the others. t:
it's about 31 degrees and all the squash is at least frozen. There is probably no recovery at this point. Green and nightshade tomatoes in the front beds survived, everything else is probably toast for this year (for us, anyway). It's possible but unlikely that the winter varieties kale and chard will make it. Heidi's peppers did, even the skin, which was impressive. The bags of young jalapenos she planted in a bag last month are also going strong. She trims those plants back often to harvest the baby chiles all through fall.

It feels like a lot, and it is. We'll get by. Harvests seem to always start with a bunch of hallelujah wins and end with a few holy sh*t losses. It's part of the game with growing, you win some you lose some. You get smart and you get better at it. This was a rough one just because we had such high hopes, and we put so much work into it. But this is only our third fall at Eastgate, and we're really just finding our legs. I'm sure it will be better next time.

Anyway, we can still have a decent Thanksgiving. Victories aren't just about volume. We are so grateful for products like Heidi's jalapenos, the tomatoes, and any greens that might make it. The tomato sauce we made yesterday with grandma's recipe is beautiful. There's so much there to appreciate. So the best thing to do now is to share this amazing food we have with each other, in the most beautiful venue on earth.

That's what I'm planning to do, and so is most of the current and many past members I've talked to. I don't know how many will come on Thursday, but I hope it's everyone who can.
Still, we could use a few volunteers to pack and deliver the food on Thursday, and anyone who wants to help with that.

t:
nothing is dead. There's enough moisture in the air that the water bottles and tarps kept the heaters going all night, and we won't find anything defrosty today. If a hard freeze really has come, it's certainly not as painful as the big numbers would suggest. If we get a lot more snow, we'll get some embedded buds in hard layers of ice and snow like we did in '78, '90 and a few others — but that's rare, and if it happened this year there would ironically be less damage from repeated thaws and refreezes than there would be this year.

My impression is that a big soft frost left some shiny bits on still-warm vegetables: Richard Shunk said that his plants died but burning themselves up with one another, mostly the green beans, squashes, melons and tomatoes. Carbon and cold burn together co-woked all the good stuff. We ate most of them anyway; they were delicious. I've lost plants to double hard freezes and triple hard freezes and all that, when we were all settled for winter and trying each year to extend the season — but those didn't make a squash that we wanted to eat undigested. It may be that many of us have uncookable winter squashes now, preserved for posterity by frost. But whether they're better raw or cooked, I can't say now; we'll know in a month or so.

The mild winter this fall has affected not just the garden's productivity but its sanity. A lot of us are getting ready to conclude we're at the ends of our gardens' seasons for this garden patch — here again, that's not as bad it once was or will be again. But two or three years ago, we had deliverance for the plants and cash using some real shifts of seasons: deep snow cover from December to the end of January, along with unexpected breaks of cold in all the months, happy seasons, the real harvest in March, dry spring weather, instant dash to birth. The warmth and light we had in January and February had more real results than we normally ever get, and that let us to say goodbye gracefully to a lot of healthy things that otherwise might have made it to this point.

Religion can take a hint, I think: some people should pay more attention to these signs than the rest of us, as well as the weather, to.)

There wasn't a whole lot of frost on the stuff that was outside. Faces of cauliflower looked like sandpaper, but still intact. Kale and escarole were white, but not flimsy or limp yet. Watermelon vines were almost totally covered in a glistening frost. Tomato leaves had that chalky brown look and the pears were all dipped in white, but the whole garden smelled fresh and the storm skittered away. That said, we did lose a few of the bell pepper plants. If you need bell pepper starts, let me know.

It's almost 40 degrees now and we can tell when sun rises. We stripped off the row covers on everything we could reach and headed in to see what we'll have to re-cover tonight. Before tomorrow we'll likely have to take a trip back out to check on everything.

nothing was harmed by the freeze, and the garden is in good shape. Some people's pepper starts dried up for what looks like a light snack, but we still have three good pepper plants and there's a lot of hope for them to make it, and for everyone else to be okay. We can account for every one of our 200+ plants. The big kohlrabi at the front was thinned, a mistake as it turns out. The majority of the crop is still small and shouldn't have been effected by the freeze. It already looked like there was enough, though, so I'm not going to stress about it, and here's the good news:

The 55 pound "giant celery" at the front is fine. I don't think I said that before. That sucker is light green, mycelly at the root but I think it's ready to be lifted right now. It's celery, not ginger, after all. We all said goodbye, but it looks like he might yet be in our Christmas Party baskets. We'll find out.

Thank you again to everyone who helped. I'm convinced, if there is ever a winter garden, we're going to try one farther up the lot.

Here's a silly little video. I had the hose running over the squash to warm it up. Since under the row covers, it's super humid, and this breaths some air in. I should probably be wearing my clothes, but I'm so old the hose keeps me warm.

http://youtu.be/P5yHr6yKK-Y?t=24s

And here's the garden this morning:

We can pick all the rest of the tomatoes now that it's been a solid 32 degrees and we can strip the vines. They've been hit with tom spots and early blight. Just like the summer crops, there will be a certain amount of produce to make things, but not like six pizzas or anything. If any of you pick up a few, especially some of the 1 pound beauties, or the hurricane san marzanos, that would be nice for this round of dinner parties.

The zucchini and summer squash were harvested as well, and will all be over for the season. I'll go fill a bin from the winter squash this morning, and see if there are any eggplants I can make it.

Meanwhile, hats off to Sylvia who, against all the odds, just pulled one last dumpster dive and snuck a handful of oranges up north last night

t:
1) The row covers and old bed sheets were not strong enough to stop the freeze in the low pasture—not all that surprising. But the trickle irrigation lines that Chris buried in the soil still appear to be up, and have protected all the pepper and okra plants. Rhonda is doing a count, but we think they all look pretty good so far. 

2) The kale, kale and kale all looks fine, surprised absolutely no damage to the 25+ beds outside this week. When I grow it, I never have a problem with a sudden cold snap, but we've had some freakier years in recent memory. 

3) The tomatoes, apparently, were too extensive for our last-ditch efforts to hold them to warmer temps. Their leaves are caked in ice. The stems on many plants are wilted or dead to the ground. I have a feeling we won't see much from them that will make it to the pantry, but we may have results. They also are covered in plastic and have seven poly (which I borrowed) over them. I'll take a torch and what I think are people who love me to them with me tomorrow to see if the inside of the plants look injured. Tomatoe stem health is the baseline for how many tomatoes make it to harvest, and when it's cold and crinkled there you know the plants are really bad off. 

The squash look okay to me at the moment, remember the heaters were on both of them last night, but it is way too late to save the remaining squash. Most of what is left (i.e. not in the dryer I bought for food prep) is going to mush in the next 24 hours, and we lost at least half a ton to the overnight freeze. Oh, well. Maybe this autumn will be year that we can get both the summer and fall harvests. 

Some of us got to go home and get some sleep. That's all.

All the chard is in, same Chinese cabbage and niniku. The kale is safe as of 6:00 AM, it's holding up just fine. It's cut back now and pretty hardy, and if it gets burned next week we can at least get the magnificent pesto deaths from it.

t:
the low temperature right here at the garden is currently 28.6, so slightly higher than the weather service prediction. (Of course, they weren't here at the garden.) All the vegetables with covers look pretty good. The kale is still perky, the tomatoes are shriveled but alive, and the dry bed area with the endive, chard, and fennel is still cold and crunchy. The whole field is good and dry from our spring rainwater retention project, so even the low areas haven't flooded much. The dahlias are all gone; not much surprise there.

The bummer news is the squash was hit hard, especially the spaghetti in the westernmost bed. All those with row covers still look pretty good; those without are, um, not so much. Jinx's pumpkin is orange but still alive. If you find yourself thinking I should have saved some of those spoiling squash for seed saving and made a big pot of mash for the cooking circle, then you and I have something in common. (On the other hand, if I were thinking that, they would be happening.)

The silver lining here is the volunteer-strong economy over the last few months has helped a lot. That's why I was out there until dark putting covers over everything. That's why Marcus David was able to put up two propane heaters in back, keeping one lighted through the coldest hour. And that's why we've been able to cover many of the beds enough to keep the mustard out. All the fans of our public gardening model had tangible concretizations this season. We even inspired another effort that is using some of our paths and roads for their own garden, Deepwell, a culinary herb garden run by a guy named Shane. A bunch of us visited with him over the summer, and it's just one more face of the farmstead's range of public chow productions that now seem inevitable. It's been a sweet peace here this summer thanks to some hotbeds and shade screens, elderly squatters and weddings. Next up: walk-in friends to pick veggies with you, roadrunner runs for river ice… I'll probably find you out there proofing leavened bread in the solar oven? Obviously we love autumn.

Some of the squash does feel like it could use another week, but everything in the ground is totally green. I suspect the little 8.6% temperature deficit just zapped the vines of some of this season's last organic mass into slummy orange legume beds,

t:
Of the five beds we covered, three had no signs of damage. Their leaves felt partly frozen, and we expect some leaves to lose winter hardiness and die over time, but the stems and buds are fine and the buds looked healthy (Earliana is a tough tomato and The Red TPS is so late it should be fine). The kales look good, too. The zucchini and summer squash flowers froze and died – who knows if that will affect the zucchini that was already ripe on Oct. 1? – but the stem and leaves look fine, as well. From reading around on the internet, it'll be hard to tell until the fruit sets or doesn't.

Two of the beds we covered, one planting of kale and one that had a variety of lettuces, had big freeze arrows and don't look so good. One bed we forgot to cover and had only the two small heaters we borrowed, and that was a total loss. 

Tuesday night we couldn't get the weather service to provide a freeze warning across Ann Arbor, so we're still not sure if the warnings released to the press were worded accurately – and Ian and Marcus had trouble with their backup plan, two propane heaters in the back beds – one stop working, and the other couldn't be moved after early freezing started to damage the greenhouses it was trying to keep warm, so it stopped heating. 

If you're thinking of being in a micro-climate war against winter, let me leave three important notes: 

1. Use rowcovers (fabric covers that are pulled over plants that trap body heat). We have saved a ton of food in the last decade using inexpensive black netting and I don't know what we'd do without it. Use whatever you can find and put it on everything you can get to before dark (though you really should do covers in an hour or two of the sun going down). Stock up on freezer bags and root cellars and cold storage.

2. In a climate war, learn how to grow "sister plants" referring to a late-blooming strain that bring produce quickly after the early bloomer. We use both Sungold and Snow White carrots – we use Sungold for family dinners but Snow White largely for the food pantry. It looks like we can grow Sungold this year, though. t:
I've got insulated row covers on the eggplant, pods of passive solar greenhouse over the aubergines, and a stack of an old sink, flower pots and the laptop covers most of our tiny pumpkin patch. That's still in. I'm covering the two big cucao downs with last year's kale crop and a hoop house top, and I emptied the compost bin and put it under the cucumbers to armor them. The compost top's an inch of rubbermaid and three layers of six-mil plastic. Those will be in as long as the sun stays down. The tomato boxes are almost completely buried under old sheet beds and covers. I'll know whether the insides came through all right tomorrow morning.

Here's where we still lost the battle: every last one of our winter squash is dead now. We tried one of the heaters on them, but we needed two running, which used twice the propane, so we left one on. What we forgot is that two of our edsquares are touching, so one didn't get the heat it needed. The rest were under the covers, so one of them got frost-free air all night, and the cold touched one quadrant of the other ones. They're shrunken up, flaccid and dead. They just don't have anything left inside.

What hit you hardest?

Where-ever; Duluths lettuce, chards and tomatoes; Viola road also.

Did you save any of your tomatoes?

Does the garden plot have an alarm system for extreme weather conditions, if not are you planning on one?

For me the crop left in the ground is always the hardest; the ones I am working on for food are the easiest and there are costs for both. Vegetables like kale aren't bothered by 50 nights with temps a few degrees below freezing. A nice garden bed of kale still produced salads two weeks before the first killing frost on record of -1 last year. With onions and garlic the challenge is to attend to what they need before they do too much robust growing. The rest of the sweet potatoes that I didn't get out early this fall won't actually die until sometime in January, if not a bit later this year since the dynamic of a tough year such as last year might have tucked in plants, as for that one night of -1 early in December there were almost no visual signs of damage.

t:
the sheet over bed 15 (the guyot tomatoes) gave out early on, it tore at the edge, so those are mostly fried. No big surprise there.

The row cover on bed 15 (the Acme and burpless squash, about half of this year's crop) is still intact, but they are in rough shape. Frost got under the cover, plants look damaged and the lower fruit is definitely done for.

The row cover on bed 16 (the fingerling potatoes) held and they look great. Potatoes can handle the cold, the leaves just look scorched. Good news there.

The row cover on bed 17 (the pumpkins) held, some frost on the leaves but nothing too bad. Fresh pumpkins are a novelty out here so we'll leave them out there for trick-or-treaters and wildlife.

The row cover on bed 18 (stretcher kale) was shot when we put it on last night, the clips weren't strong enough so it tore down the middle when the wind picked up, so all the kale is shot.

The covers on the raised beds with chard, kale and kale seedlings held and the hight helped, but they are cold, maybe even cooked, so if they survive that's great. It wouldn't be the first year we lost the whole fall chard and kale crop.

And that's for vegetables. For fruits: the Coveralls and half of bed 8 (atarik and kebar bananas and the Ruby Red) were covered, they're still cold but not cooked so we'll see. The rest of the banana bed was too windy to cover and they're fried. Taquari apples, same thing, the cover held and they're cold but still good so we'll see.

One more thing, the plastic under the big banana bed is compromised and the bed is flooded. The garden crew is working out an alternate water management plan in consultation with the Comp Plan Commission that will address this bed and its effect on surrounding beds. More as it develops.

Sorry for the bad news. Would anyone like one or two pumpkins? We'll probably take in too many.

t:
all the tomatoes, every one, were iced. I was afraid they would be, so I cut the last green balls off, stuck them in the cooler, and now they're just cold and not dead. We'll see if they survive. One of the kale rows was fine; the other was iced. I picked the clean leaves off and brought them in, but it looks like they're done for. The chard is tote road for real. I cryed like a baby. In the pollinator beds, every plant down for the winter is toast, every one. It's a really pretty garden now, though, lots of color, lots of blossoms; the bees didn't notice. In the back beds where the bedsheets protected the squash in the low spots, everything survived, both the pumpkins and the zucchini varieties. Around 85% in the big bed with the plastic and the heater, and 100% in the two back beds where it was warmer.

Joanne said the pantry appreciates what we send, but half is better than none. We learned a lot in this first freeze, and we'll try to do better next year, find the coldest spot for the tomatoes, use the heaters and the bedsheets for the kale, hit or miss.

Back to bed. This garden will need a lot of work before summer.

Big hugs,
Karen

t:
• The kale is toast — totally brown, even the stuff on the south-facing slope or under row covers.  
• The chard is still good in the spots with covers, but the broomcorn style is not very cold-hardy and didn't survive the night on the ground.  
• The tomatoes look like they survived, but they were a little soft, so we're bringing the big ones in and saving the cherry ones for another day. We'll see if they make it.

All of the winter squash still good, sealed tight in their little igloos on the creek bank, except for the acorn squash on the bottom slope — lost every one of them. Not a single crookneck or buttercup is still out or good, so that's the end of the line for the summer squash season. But we still have 20 sugar pumpkins that all look good, and so far none of the butternuts got any damage. Looking to the spring, we also still have the broccoli and cauliflower, all our storage onions, both planters of carrots and the bed of kohlrabi.

So that's the freeze in a nutshell.

Starting tomorrow we'll be cleaning out the smaller beds and going through the compost to bail out any survivors. Like I said up top, this was a big source of fresh veggies for our partners at St. Brendan's, so we'll be dropping off what we have. We'll bring an empty box for anyone who wants to take some.

Much as this sucks, we still have a lot of good food. Please look over the list above and sign up for a slot if you want to help gather it all up and take it over (Wednesday after 2 p.m.). If you have a vehicle and want to help with deliveries, let me know — you'd need a valid driver's license and insurance.

Like I said, you've all done an amazing job this year and we even got in a few watermelons. We'll get through this, and next year will be even better.

the beans are all toast; the kale and the collards looked him, too. The kale leaves did look wilted this morning, but they all perked up by lunchtime and had no burn or browning. The peppers are good; the tomatillos are good; the tomatoes are perfect which surprised me because they were still bare. The squash fared best of all, and all of this matches what we saw yesterday afternoon.

In the beds with low spots we pulled out bunches of spinach before the freeze (voluminous, leafy bunches) and it all froze in the unheated walk-in cooler. That's not salvageable, but otherwise the refrigerated cold storage held better than I expected. The stuff we're not sure about we put out to warm up.

I suppose it could get worse yet but it's looking like we'll be short the beans, the collards, the kale, about two thirds of the tomatoes, and maybe 5-10% of the squash. The rest looks great. In the large scheme of things that's a good return, except of course for all the time spent fighting the freeze.

Postscript from Ruth -- she's headed out to bring warm layers to anyone she spots heading out to fight the freeze; we're guessing that's a few hundred of us across Dupage County.

all of the beds that weren't covered and a few that were are either destroyed or greatly damaged; I counted at least 40 buttersquash plants, seven black maxis and six ambers lost. The beds with row covers or sheets were not hit as hard, although we think a few sheets blew off for part of the night, so we'll check this morning for more damage. Big shout-out to Joanne at the food pantry for coming over to help and treat for frostbite while we covered everything early on, to Marcus for setting up the heaters and to the ten of you who showed up to help at two in the morning, and thanks to everyone else who donated supplies to make it work. We'll likely be giving what's left of both crops to Mal's Farm Stand tomorrow. Also, we're still looking for two more hay bales to get the plants off the ground (putting them between plants makes heaters circulate warm air better). They have to be off the ground; we can't stack stuff on top of them.

Thanks also to all the Central Quivira League members who donated hay for the garden this year. We'll see what shape things are in once the sun comes up.

t:
_read more_

We saved almost everything. Just a handful of wilted kale and some chewed-up leaves on the collards. A little stunted growth on the winter squash, but nothing lost. Tomatoes are a few degrees warmer so they're fine. And vining crops like pole beans, cucumbers and melons all did well under their little tent we're trying out.

Digging in tonight by flashlight is actually pretty magical. We have these 30-foot towers of rows overhead with covers and sheets draped like sails between them. It's like the garden is all underwater. I keep thinking it's going to snow any second, just because that's what a soft red light and the hush at this hour makes me think. Jason had to laugh when I asked if we'd be okay, if this little camp would be warm enough, and he said "Not for long, right?"

No, it's mid-December and we're not going to survive out here forever. Our heating bill went from $20 a month to just under $100 last night to keep the propane tanks gurgling, which we're not really set up to pay. We're lucky people, though: next year our loan comes through, and then we'll all be sweating like pigs in the new greenhouses. Until then, it's a few glasses of whiskey and a little hope, and another day of spring in the middle of winter.

It's been a long week. How's it standing out there?

t:
- Greens: All the kale and chard are either dead or salad-thin. Really tough to see losing that much. The collards in the south bed look better (something to do with how low they are and the protection from row covers), but not much.

- Root vegetables: Lots of damage in the northeast bed--all of the storing onions are mush, and both the carrot patch and the Daikon turnips have lots of ice damage. We had covered them with an extra thick game of mulch (leaves, straw, grass clippings) under sheets, but it still wasn't enough to stop the ice. The carrots look worse than the turnips, though a few on the outside edge survived.

- Beans and peas: They're living! The snow peas behind the shed and on the east side of the trellis are still alive, and there's a handful of purple beans that made it through on the side of the trellis by the turnaround. The knee-high's under the row cover behind the shed look alive, and the mysterious patch of green you asked about yesterday by the back fence are living too--looks like something survived in the low spot behind the back fence.

- Tomatoes: The two heaters and the row cover behind them worked--they're still healthy, and we're even getting a few more green tomatoes.

- Winter squash: The heat and row covers protected all but the98% of the winter squash looks great and only a bit of wilting is showing. Just keep an eye on it over the next few days. The zucchini and pumpkins will likely need a little trellis help to keep them off the ground.

We'll be deciding over the next few days what, if anything, we can salvage from the fall greens and roots. There's a unplanned-for gap in the pantry's supplies this year.  I'll likely be shopping for collard greens at Safeway to fill in some of the gap for them. 

The good news is the spring crops look great. We're already harvesting radishes (pun intended) from the cold frames, and the beds are ready to go. We'll get them in this week. If you're a winter gardener, there's still time to apply for an indoor bed this year.

The bed of butternut squash made it with only minimal damage; nothing lost in the front bed that's over most of the winter squash except the acorn squash, of which we only got six good ones. All the tomatoes died, but most of them were already showing signs of going anyway.

Long story short, we lost some food, but we saved most of it -- and we'll have enough left over to donate to St. Brendan's. For now the garden will be closed.

And now, because I know some of you are probably interested, here are the as-yet-unaudited results of the second annual KZOO listener survey.
