t:
all the row covers and sheets are still in place (thanks to pretty much wasting all my tape and strings on them yesterday). The stone rows and the big tomatoes are all under them. I should say 'a slight frost coating'; there were a few spots where the leaves touched a little, but nothing that indicates any damage. The tomatoes are still a little green, but sturdy; sturdy as in the main stems, not the fruit, and they shouldn't be out any longer, so we might need to cut back some. (Can someone actually check the main stems: there's a few large ones that are a little soft.)

I think we'll be okay. Emphasis on think, not know. All those beds under covers came out dry on my inspection, and no damage to the squash. (I think that's a first: I've heard a number of horror stories about propane heaters, and this one went well.) No water on the ground means no tipburn, which in that newsletter from 1963 Joanne gave me yesterday could happen after a heavy freeze.

If anyone is starting to finish planning their fall crops, planning ahead for a mention in the newsletter. I need Carol or Patty to set the calendar at St. Brendan's. Carol is running rockets on Saturday from 10 until 2 (thanks on that, Carol), so I was thinking a Saturday morning get-together sometime between then and Christmas — dates on the actual signs start appearing now. She can post on the bulletin board and Patty can announce it at the tables if we can firm one down. Carol had mentioned sometime near Thanksgiving, but I don't know if people would be focused enough after the shopping frenzy. The holidays are really getting busy around here, and I know people with many obligations.

Hope everyone slept well and I hope to hear about those monster tomatoes.

Karen Whitley

t:
A generous frost last night blackened all of our spinach, which looks dead, and the broccoli which was just starting to make heads. The small cut-and-come-again lettuce bed can still be salvaged, but will have to be harvested small and quickly. The chard looks unhappy--I don't know if we'll get any more good leaves. The kale is a disaster; I'll be pulling the blackened stuff today, and maybe there will be a decent core in the middle with a few more days' luck.

The peppers, cucumbers, and tomatoes still look good, and everything alive is safely under cover. I'll stay on the garden overnight with a flashlight and maybe a thermos of hot tea and do as much damage control as I can. Marc will check in after sunrise. But if it gets below freezing again, no matter what we do, I think the garden's done.

When the sun comes up, we'll see how things are. Tomorrow night we'll be back pulling and salvaging whatever we can for St. Brendan's to have something to supplement everybody's canned goods.

t:
-- Tomatoes: Some leaves blackened yesterday on the undersides next to the trunks, but didn't look much different this morning. We brought in all the cherries that were still hanging and finished the Roma harvest, but the rest of the Romas, San Marzanos and heirlooms didn't ripen and won't make it. The three Lehmeisters we've tried to save in raised beds are still out, but probably done for.
-- Kale: Regrowth all green this morning. The leaves that were blackened yesterday look yellowish now but still firm.
-- Chard: Still out in the beds. Blanched just a bit last night. Will check again later.
-- Winter squash: Mostly looks OK. Some minor blanching on the zucchinis, but all still firm. Yellow squash looks fine. 
-- Pumpkins: Affected the same as squash. Big One looks fine.
-- Onions: Still out, and green onions coming along under the new cloches. The low ground near the creek edge is browned at the tips but perky on the parts under the cloche and on the ridge.
-- Mirliton (chayote): Still ripening. A few leaves blackened last night, but new leaf growth looks good this morning and fruits are still firm. 
-- Sweet potatoes: Not growing much this late in the season, but overall look good. 
-- Peppers: Still hanging in there. Some leaves blackened, but new reds emerged along with yesterday's rain.
-- Beds: Most of our beds were covered by theawnstorm, though three floating row covers came loose an flapped around in the wind and tore a bit. Two solid cloches held fast in the lower yard but toppled over in the upper beds. 
-- Heaters: We shut the heaters off about 2 a.m. when the temperature held at 30. I just measured 35 degrees by the Creek beds, so the heaters are staying off until it warms up. When I checked, each heater was using a little over 2.1 gallons since they were lit yesterday afternoon. We don't have any more on hand, but Joanne offered to get more today if anyone would like to help her take a look this evening. 

Thanks again to everyone who showed up last night. We'll meet to assess again after 5 p.m. When we do decide to bring the tomatoes in early, we'll need hands to process them for canning

No tomatoes, none of the yellow squash, and none of the kale and chard. Those leaves are the color of frozen spinach. All that's still green are the winter squash, and Joanne says we can leave those for pickup tomorrow for all she cares, as her crew is already looking forward to cooking with them. I'll sweep them for any stragglers tomorrow morning.

So, half a garden. But church tomato soup and squash chili starts tomorrow, and I know we'll have lots of willing hands from the congregation. If you're free, please come help us cook up the garden."

t:
tomato advisor: The heater by the steak tomatoes (~75 plants, caprese & san marzano types) did its job. Every green tomato still on the vine is fine, and nothing got frostbitten. It looks like we'll have enough to make sauce, maybe do an outdoor tomato pie or something from the culls. Kale & chard: I designed a goofy system to keep things warm with the two portable heaters, trying to get at least 6-8 inches of air space between the bottom of the plants and the heat. That worked. We lost maybe a dozen plants total; that's the background level of loss for our kale+chard in the fall. Winter squash: got a little iffy with the weather service's wind chill estimates, but temperatures stayed safely above freezing. We just have a few frostbitten spots on leaves -- no loss.

More good news: I heard from Judy and Nate at the Guilford Coop's Roots & Shoots program. They're headed to the farm tomorrow morning, coming from XVII Crew with enough volunteer power to help us harvest. They'll give us a hand with the tomato pie project, then head home to get their farms' fall harvest ready for Southeast Elementary (they school their own kids in the afternoon).

Other projects in the works that could use a hand if anyone's got time: stopping byCONN for a repeat of the apple cider pressing on October 26th (me + one more), sowing fall cover crops along the creek footpath and in the expansion bed, harvesting our crop of baby turnips, and compost turning.

If you'd like to help with any of those, let me know. In the meantime, thanks again to everyone who braved the cold to protect those plants. And very special thanks to Marcus, our unofficial safety officer, for doing the heater installs.

t:
everything in our back two beds was toasted. The beds came off, plastic melted under them and one of the beds ignored the law of gravity and jumped a fence. Hill's wideCOMMuter 542 aka Rockati, who lives just above the garden and takes good care of his plants, lost two new raised beds in his yard.  

The north side of the middle bed was hit hard. The south side, facing one heater, is okay. You can see the line. Kale got nuked on one side, not the other. Most of the vines stayed warm enough, but the leaves on the north side were co-opted by frost. The tomatillos got hit on the north and up close, but okay farther away. 

I can't find Marcus's phone or we'd have a frost-burned-fingers check-in to post here.

Everyone  whose names I saw on yesterday's comments can reclaim credit for whatever happened to survive. Special shout-outs tofungigrl (Wylla) for being the first on the scene and bumpersprint (Dieter) for bringing space heater batteries and muscleguy (Mike) for his star turn holding a heated gun up into the winter squash vines (and for encouraging us not to stir them in the morning). ymc(Config) and jbrand (Jenna) ran around putting covers on everything that could be covered. Joanne (of the St. B's pantry) and kevin (Kevin) got there early, too. For everybody, thank you. If you spotted something I missed, let me know and we'll put you on the credit roll.

If you're not a member and want to help the garden recover, we'll be out there next week putting up a cold frame and planning for spring crops (spinach, kale, greens). We have a lot of folks on the volunteer list now, and it's open to anyone who gardens regularly, so if you're interested in joining us and I haven't seen you around with a rake lately, you're welcome. Just let me know.

Thanks to all of you, garden members and not, for your concern, advice and help with the garden this year.

t:
hard freeze, down to 30. It's snowing a little. Not a lot, maybe half an inch.

The beds with sheet mulch and straw mulch are fine. Root crops in the insulation bed (beets and parsnips) look good. The beds with kale, chard and winter squash beneath tulip poplars are cold, because the trees block the heat of the ground and the mulches aren't as thick. A couple leaves are blackened and limp, but no widespread damage. I moved the coldest eggplant to the greenhouse. I didn't see any fresh damage on all the fall tomatoes under rows of plastic, but I did find one tomato with a bunch of little fruits starting, probably from pollinating about three weeks ago. Maybe a miracle.

The final update will come in the morning, when my flashlight can show me more than a yard or two of cold garden. We're lucky this was early, because the forecast is for no cold snaps for the rest of the winter. Hang in there.

t:
most of the squash looks okay, although a few plants succumbed. I'm counting so I can call that in as a deduction from last month's garden yield. One of the heaters burned out, but the other three areas were warm enough -- the kale and the new chard that was starting to come in turned translucent, but was otherwise fine, and the second heater is still going.

The tomatoes are another story. We did a late blight watch, and six of the thirty-two plants are showing signs [great link for anyone who hasn't seen it: http://www.gardenfundamentals.com/vegetable-gardening-preventing-early-blight.html]. We wintered over a lot of tomato starts, but the only variety that seemed cold-hardy was Sun Gold. We were also hoping for Green Zebras, but they only made it until the fourth of July. The Sun Golds were so good that we kept not taking any in, so that's probably why we have late blight, but I don't regret it. I hadn't planned on canning so many tomatoes, but I sent Sarah home with a bucket.

Where this gets tricky is that St. Brendan's also gets some tomatoes from the Abbey soup kitchen. I helped move those a couple of times, and they'd hate to lose this week's. So we'll be splitting. Joanne is volunteering to drive a couple of trips and back up my pick of the good tomatoes. That means I get to decide which tomatoes go to the pantry and which go in our freezer for sauce. If anyone wants to help can, let me know. Now that the crew is used to the scent of our kitchen, I'll bet we get volunteers.

The kale and new chard both look good, and that's turning into a question of who wants it. Joanne said there are still some mouths to feed at the food pantry, and there are folks who walk the back roads picking up vegetables we leave out. depending on who shows up, I'll put out the coded signs that mean kale for the chow line or the private pile. 

I figure no matter who gets the kale, we'll be starting the winter chard and new spring peas next week, so the garden yields will ramp up again. Hopefully with colder nights instead of one long heat spell.

t:
Back beds--surprisingly unscathed, for the most part. A little damage to the tomatoes, but the kale held up, and the spinach bed is in good shape. It looks like the row cover protected everything from the dirt mulch up. There was still ice on the heater above the tomatillos, and the tomatoes hanging under the bedsheet had ice on them, but they look ok.

Down in the gully--sad. There's still a little squash down there to pick, and plenty left on the vines. All the kale we planted in the gully is frozen, though, what little isn't already submerged in the creek. I'll walk down along the creek with sebuah_gift tomorrow, and I put up a sign at Main Street knowledge so people know to take anything still salvagable. PLEASE don't take any squash that's been frozen, unless you're making soup and don't care if it's 50% water. The tomatoes should all be picked at this point; anyone can take those.

Others will be welcome to stay out and pick the better of the winter squash left. I'll leave the row covers off the beds at the gate so people can get in early to grab produce before it freezes solid. It's good stuff, maturing as hard as granite.

The last of the outputs sadly had to go. I feel sick about it. Some of the worst crop losses I've ever seen. First freeze in about ten years, and the uh... weedy? Competition wasn't stellar this year either. But it'sTuesday; there's still about twenty feet of decent row cover, and another fifty feet of sheeting somewhere, that we can put to use in the spring. Thank you again to everyone who braved the weather to help us.

t:
golden broccolini is shot; those were out in the open for early birds. But the kale looks great, and even our late tomatoes are doing okay, along with sow thistles and some wild mustard that came up behind the tomatoes. I think we'll have carrots under the mulch in a day or two, and the storage onions are all up and looking good. Most of these were under covers or row covers, or with bedsheets over them. It was 29 when I put my gloves on, so about a degree above freezing. Last night's wind died down just as the temperatures fell, which helped a lot. No loss of the beets – we clumped them close together between the bedsheets.

We'll know more as the day goes on. I'm going to sit by the propane heater and see whether it's actually warm enough next to the squash to help, and whether the one at the tomatoes is too hot.

I wasn't planning to go into the house and warm up, but I'm sure glad it's there this morning. I plan to make a big pot of coffee when it's light, and start warming up on the wood stove to dry out my gloves. We'll see whether my tomatoes, kale and onions can make it through the second half of the night before we know how much we have to replace. I'll post updates as I get them.

Hang in there, folks. The wind calmed, and this garden made it through the '90s, so maybe we'll luck out this time, too.

Half the tomatoes that were closest to the ground froze. We only have an hour or two of daylight, but Jo says she's coming down if the sun thaws things enough to pick the rest. If the sun doesn't come through, we'll pick what we can reach and quarter the rest. We can still save some of those.

We'll give what's good and throw the rest in the compost bin; our two neighbors and the Sodexho guys on the_other_side_of_the_creek are getting a lot of extra compost this month.

The kale and chard were iced up solid. That's a shame, but it's not worth the gas to run the heaters all night. We'll toss that after the sun comes up.

All of the winter squash looks good, and the last of the peppers. The onions froze, so we'll toss those. Four others we'd been babying through the summer are still hanging on, but not worth heating.

Biggest surprise: the baby tomatoes in that house never dropped below 36. I'll never convince myself that one layer of newspaper and a sheet was enough, but the rest of that batch is fine.

Worst case, we basically lose the back half of the garden, 18 beds. I know people like to brag, and the brag here would be the double harvest, but we never had a brag post last year. We learned to use all the space we could when we helped out the Lettuce were_Hurricane_Irene_damaged_guys last year, and that's one reason we had more than last year. Sometimes things go a different way. We'll take what surprises us and figure out how to work with it.

That's all for now. I'll try to get a photo post up when we figure out what's still good down there, after sunrise.

t:
all the watermelons covered by the plastic are fine -- the row covers protected them well enough. The kale is still a bit crunchy on the edge, but should be ok. The collard greens covered with bedsheets in the front bed were in the low 30s when I checked this morning -- below freezing but not at the bottom of the scale. The beds with tomatoes and peppers are a little colder where the sheets didn't overlap, with one or two tomato leaves blackened on the edges. On the other hand, the blocks of cucumbers and chard that only got row covers and no heaters are all intact -- the row covers made that much difference. The lone butternut squash in the hoop house has some frost on its leaves but looks alive. And surprise: the acorn squash we left uncovered as a test look ok, too. The leaves have browned at the edge but the stems are still green, and there doesn't look to be any rot on the fruits yet.

So it looks like we saved most of the winter squash, all of the melons, almost all the greens, and most of the tomatoes and peppers, with copper penny damage to a few leaves (more manageable than if they'd frozen and burst). We lost a few of the cucumbers that were outside the row covers, and we'll see how the basil comes back from its cold bath, but that's probably all.

Perhaps the best news: we caught Ben on his way out and he gave us his last two portable propane heaters. Marcus put them on the bed of peppers and eggplant. Could make the difference between life and death for those peppers, and protect the basil too.

So that is as good as it could have been, and not just because we were lucky with the cover material. A big, big thank you to everyone who dropped what they were doing to pull everything together before the temperature dropped, and a huge thank you to Joanne and everyone at St. Brendan's for making the donation drop-off so much easier this year. Those are the things that make a difference when there's only a narrow window to work in.

Also, if anyone has more drop cloths or spare bedsheets, we could use every scrap we can find before the next cold snap.

t:
*  No heat on the front bed for technical reasons — it's on a corner and the wind comes straight through there, so putting a cover on it would be like anchoring a sail. Instead we piled an extra wheelbarrow and the rain barrel over it and aimed both heaters that way. It held the cold off, but not by much. We lost pretty much everything in the front bed except the ugly-but-tasty volunteer winter squash and a lone purple okra plant that somehow survived. 

*  Back beds did better. The hoops protected the covers well, so everything there made it. (Photo: see next post in your feed.) We still lost the pumpkin that had hidden under the row cover, but its neighbor protected the cukes and zucchinis next to it well enough that they're viable. The kale, chard and tomatoes lost a few leaves, but everything still looks alive. I brought the heaters around after they warmed up the winter squash patch, and that seemed to help.

*  The hot bed with the new seedlings held. A little chilly, but not too bad.

Bottom line: we have about half the crop I was hoping for, and lost almost everything we won't be able to replace from seed saved on site. The resilient volunter winter squash — the little knobby orange gourds — have been picked and brought inside. 

We'll need to make up the shortfall to St. Brendan's somehow, so I'm looking at the community-supported agriculture shares we'll start next year and seeing if we can bring that date up. If anyone has friends with greenhouses or Basmati rice to donate, let me know.

For now, the garden needs a day off. Thank you, everyone, for helping. It's not the result we hoped for, but it could have been a lot worse and we did everything we could. Tomorrow I'll be looking for volunteer hands to scrape the dead leaves and set up the cold frames under the hoophouse for winter planting — anyone who wants to join, drop me a note. My main job is wrangling a battalion of Trick-or-Treaters, but I'm sure there will be work to do in the garden that doesn't require a scarily good aim with a nerf dart gun. 

Be well and stay warm.

(The kale and chard next to the fence somehow escaped. They're a little mushy but still green.) I know it's not fresh from the garden but in this economy, canned, jarred and frozen food can help a lot of families. t:
Ended up there was still some frost on the southern-facing part of the beds, and about 99% of the leafy greens we were trying to protect are black and crispy. I learned yesterday that kale can stand a little frost and bounce back, but this isn't that little. Also down are the eggplants and peppers Somebody dug out yesterday afternoon to use up what was left. Sorry, BMI.

Good news: the onions, garlic, carrots and most of the parsnips didn't have any frost, my guess because their tops are low to the ground and close to the soil. So we'll have something to share. Also everything under row covers held up fine, including the biggest tomato plants, and the heaters kept the soil under the bed warm enough that the tomatoes apparently kept photosynthesizing through the night. (They're standing up and looking green.) So we'll have tomatoes. I'll harvest as much as I can for the pantry in the morning.

Bad news: One of our two heaters ran out of propane overnight. Not enough left in the tank to keep the back bed above freezing, and since the tomatoes are set up to trail over that back bed, I shut it off to keep anyone from getting carbon monoxide poisoning. (Yes, you can get CO poisoning from a propane heater running out of fuel in an unventilated space.) If the freeze persists, I may have to move the plants to where the other heater is.

That's the situation. I'll post again this afternoon once we know how the rest of the night went. If any of you hear of neighbors who have extra propane tanks, let me know. Gonna be freezing every night until at least Thanksgiving.

— K

I'm so, so relieved. You are welcome to come and see for yourselves if you're up early. As soon as it's light enough we'll pick the tomatoes, wash and box the kale and chard, and bring it all to the pantry. 

Meanwhile -- so grateful to our volunteer meteorologist Devin, to Joanne at the pantry, to Marcus and his family for the use of the heaters, and especially to everyone else who got out there last night in the dark. Thank you. That's the sort of thing you don't think a community garden needs until it does.

............................
8:13 AM - This morning's harvest is in. The tomatoes are solid. I had to gently squeeze some of the lower fruit to check and it was just fine inside. We picked 35 lbs, so about half our usual fall harvest but we'll take it 100%. The kale and chard are also fine, about 50 bunches total.

Marcus is out back now loading them into his truck to deliver to St. Brendan's -- every pound counts for them, Joanne said. I'll post photos later of this go-round. For now I'm just grateful and grateful and grateful. 

More later, after some coffee.

 onions: We lost quite a few in the central bed closest to the creek. The ones closer to the top of the hill are looking okay. We'll see when the leaves unfurl this morning.

t:
• My yard, the two raised beds right outside the garden gate. Those two propane heaters did their job. In a world where that's the happy ending, I'll take it — next year I'm definitely wrapping those beds in spunbond. Of course it's a different story out in the garden.

• The kale and chard on the south side under the willow tree. Heavy frost, almost all the leaves killed, but green is showing where the stems aren't buried in leaf litter. Most of it will bounce back, but it's a couple of weeks away — they were our last tomatoes' companion planting.

• All the carrots. We'd pulled most of them during last week's harvest, but there were some late, tiny ones still in the ground. They're in. 

• The winter squash. The two butternut vines in the east bed are pruned right up to the pumpkins, both plants completely encased in frost but and still standing. We covered them with both fabric and two layers of old bedsheets that were tied down with twine so they wouldn't fly off in the wind. I found both pumpkins intact and firm — they are COLD but not yet damaged. A few beads of condensation on the surface, but no killing discoloration. This is a *very* narrow escape. Thank you to everyone who stayed past dark to make that happen.

• Theusual Suspects. We put a sheet over the main marquee bed and Joanne's two zucchini plants in the back. Could only get one heater to their area, the wind had the other one blowing around dangerously. Checking on it now, all the leaves are pretty frosted but still upright, plants seem alive underneath. Again, it's cold, not dead. breathed a mammoth sigh of relief on that one.

t:
(1) the mini-heaters worked. The flower beds near the south fence are touch-and-go, but alive, and okay to the touch. The big beds with the winter squash are nice and toasty. (2) The kale, collards and tomatoes are...not so lucky. Looks like about half of the plants I covered with plastic either froze or got hammered by the wind and snapped/broke. Green kale is like a big flag out there, catches the wind. Some of our biggest kale is gone. The tomatoes that were still ripening on the vine were protected under plastic, but the unsubmerged roots look... sad. I couldn't get any of the leaves to unfurl—the stems are soft.

Here's the good news: the winter squash, the garlic, and the chard (I wrapped the whole row with tarp and some coconut coir, held it down with soil anchors), look fine. And the pepper plants are still looking good. I'll stay out there at sunrise and see if the flower buds have survived. If they have, they should be okay for the rest of the winter.

We'll know more tomorrow after the sun comes up. In the meantime, I'll see if anyone wants to help me re-cover the tender things—the kale, tomatoes, and still-hopeful pepper plants—and double up the anchors.

Hang in there, everyone. Thanks as always to everyone who showed up last night to protect the garden. If anyone wants to take a few minutes to help me re-cover the plants tonight, I'll be back in the next hour or so.

—Karen

t:
The covers held on all night and the plants underneath look okay. Tomatoes, especially the green fruit, look a bit frostbitten, but the old leaves that would have been browned anyway are browned and the new growth looks intact.

Kale and chard leaves were crinkled but the stems are okay, no obvious damage. We lost the crap leeks that were still in the ground, which nobody's sad about. The main beds of winter squash (hubbard, kabocha and butternut) made it, and_ack_ the baby gourds for some reason were totally unaffected. They didn't even have droop this morning, which I thought was bizarre until I realized there are still a few of them nestled under the runner beans, which were protected inside the high tunnel. collateral damage for the beans (see below) but I'll take that trade.

The cold did get into the tunnels though, and two outside beds that we hadn't pulled up (heirloom carrots and Egyptian walking onions) were fried. We were planning to pull those anyway and turn under cover crops, so it's less of a loss although it means we have to wait for next year's seeds to sprout. 

Marcus checked the Rip Van Winkle pump in the greenhouse and said it's still working, although it was lukewarm at first thing this morning. Our (limited) seed stock is safe and so is the massive quantity of dogwood cuttings we stuck in the greenhouse wet wall last month.

There are a _lot_ of dead bees out front, which sucks, and I'm pretty sure we're going to lose the apple tree out by the front gate. But overall this was a hell of a lot better than it could have been, and we have enough winter squash that even the volunteers who can't stand it (hi, Joanne) won't be able to avoid it.

A couple of action items for today:
* If anyone wants to scrounge up a dozen or so bad but usable tomatoes, I'll bring them by the back door at St. B's after vespers and you can pick them up
* The cover crops in the back field are looking a little sparse. Does anyone want to direct-seed clover or winter rye in the empty spots? We have seed on hand if you do.

Thanks to everyone who showed up last night, and thanks again to Marcus for wrangling the heaters.

t:
*   Almost every jalapeño is gone, but we saved a few. (They make it through nicer freezes than we predicted.) We'll see how they look in another week, but they've lost most of their flower buds.
*   Winter squash is still hanging and untouched on top, although it's sure to get stunted by frost.
*   The long green beans looks OK.
*   All the direct-sowed spring greens have turned brown at ground level and look gone. These included some spinach in the hoop house and both our main beds of kale and chard planted after the July 4 storm. That's the saddest damage for me personally, because it was my first time growing those.
*   The crops we sowed in containers and pots are all OK, even the ones off the ground on the porch. I moved all the basil plants and the little tomatoes that weren't in ground beds onto the porch, and they're fine.
*   Tomatoes in the ground are uniformly wilted and brown except for two plants that are still standing. They were the Black Krim, grown from saved seeds. There must be something about that strain -- Joanne said hers have been the last to go every fall for years.
*   The main crop of garlic is still down in the ground and looks untouched, although of course we won't know for sure until we dig it in a few weeks.

The heaters went out around 5 a.m., when the propane ran out. After that the beds that were still uncovered had only a few leaves left on them by dawn. The row covers and bedsheets held heat remarkably well overnight, at least compared to what I remember from the big freeze in 2010, when we lost almost everything that didn't have a greenhouse to hide in.

We can be grateful for what we saved and for the people who came out to help. Health and safety first, always, but I'm proud of us for putting in the work to save what we could. And many thanks to Daniel and Catherine for the heaters.

Now it's on to planning the spring crop. We've got a couple workshops already on the calendar, and it's harvest- and seed-saving time for the fall crops that survived. We also need to lay some drains if we hope to grow in the same beds next year.

Please join us forCoffee and PlanningThursday at 9 a.m.just down by the garden shed. Bring your mug, if you like. We'll talk about how to regroup after the freeze

t:
* The row covers held in most of the warmth we generated. We only lost a few outer leaves on the kale and chard, and maybe a tip or two of broccoli. (Longtime readers know I'm convinced row covers work miracles — with a few sacrifices.) The broccoli and chard, both in_family Cruciferae_, were the most sensitive to the cold, probably because these genotypes are from Mediterranean ancestors. 

* The tomatoes are a sad story though. Even sheltered by a black plastic bedsheet and the propane heater directly behind them, they froze last night. This is the first time I've ever lost tomatoes to a freeze, and I doubt it will be the last. If we're going to get any fall crop, we'll start pulling the red ones that are at least a bit ripe starting tomorrow morning, and we'll see what we can save of the smaller green ones by bringing them into the greenhouse.

* They got down to 28 degrees in the garden, which is just above the threshold for winter squash. I pulled back the row cover to check the vines, and they seemed alive but kept shivering. After I re-covered them and the next few rows, I saw steam come off the wet soil for a long time, which was a good sign the roots weren't hitting the lethal 24 degrees of a killing frost. I'll know more after daybreak, but I'm a little more optimistic about the squash now.

* The garlic, having gone through a killing frost already, has stored nutrients in its bulb, so I'm less worried about it. We'll be digging next week.

* No losses yet in the greenhouse: everything leafy (lettuce, peppers — though I've started to bolt a few outside — and the tropical herbs not yet rooted) is still looking good, and the tomatoes in there might survive to give us a final crop of Roma sauce. It's worth trying for a few days to see if the fruit will ripen. I'll move _Sungolds_ and any other still-green _indeterminates_ into the greenhouse tomorrow.

* Photosynthetic rates slow down at these temperatures, so photosynthesis pretty much stops when it's 42 and below. That is not a friendly environment for plants! But the row covers create enough of a greenhouse effect that the temperature under them was 10-20 degrees higher than the air temperature, and our little heaters in the bed helped even more. t:
Some good news: the one thunderstorm some of you stayed up for last week did the garden a huge favor, filling the creek and soaking the soil as deep as the roots on our hillside. All that moisture made the plants a lot more cold-hardy, so we lost less than I feared.

*
The bad news: we lost a lot anyway. The kale and chard that came up late — those big bright-blue pots — were toast (literally, sorry). Everything near the creek that wasn't insulated on all four sides, plus the edge rows of cabbage and broccoli. The tomatoes took a hit, and even under burlap I'm seeing frost burn on the bottom leaves of a couple of the big beefsteaks. Half the winter squash is gone, which is the hardest — most of those were almost ready for the pantry and nearly all the fruit we'd planned to give away is gone.

The good news in the squash losses is that the ones protected by two layers of covers survived. I'll pick those tomorrow and get them into the pantry tomorrow afternoon if they hold. If not, we'll set up the big insulated box to keep the good ones from freezing tonight.

I'll also rescue anything left in the kale and chard (the big centered patch in the yellow pot with the scarecrow is okay). And I expect most of the garlic will be fine — Anything under three inches of mulch survived out front.

You guys know this garden better than anyone, so take a few minutes and stop by if you want to help me triage what stays in the ground and what I should pull now. Anything that's still green after a light scratch is probably okay to leave, but don't plant anything tender for at least a week — the ground will be too cold. Joanne at St. Brendan's is great about using greens in soups, so we'll give her what we can and fill in the gaps at the store. It's always a learning year.

One last note for the spring planners: the pump in the main bed broke. It was starting to rattle in August, and when the temp dropped it seized up completely. I bypassed it for the irrigation, but figures a hard freeze would be the thing that breaks the last frost-proof part we had. (There's a spare in the shed when we can get to town.) Anyway, just a head's-up that won't work until we repair it. We'll start that as soon as we can get back in.

- Heaters work, but only on a tiny area. We may look at more for next time if we can coordinate fuel safely.
- Row covers are fast to put on and good for a few degrees of protection, but not enough on their own during a hard freeze.
- Bedsheets are a last-ditch measure and not reliable; better than nothing, but only for short-term protection.
- Having scheduled shifts and an updated contact list for emergencies helps a lot. credit to Jo and Marcus for pulling a late shift after closing up the store.

We'll count what we can salvage in the morning. Please check the sign-up sheet if you're available for sorting for the pantry. If anyone wants to coordinate a community "de-freeze and prep" day next weekend, that would be a huge help. I'll bring coffee.

Thanks to everyone who pitched in, and to the few who texted me at midnight with embellished freeze survival stories. This garden is only as strong as the people in it.

t:
- The peppers (in those big raised beds with black plastic sides) all survived, protected by 4 mil landscape plastic we'd put up as windbreak last spring.
- All the bush beans under row covers made it. The ones without protection didn't.
- Rows under the old screen frames (the kale, most of the chard and the small tomatoes) all protected by bedsheets, did OK. There's some frost burn on the kale crowns, but it looks healthy.
- The transplanted Fall Rhapsody tomatoes in the sunroom were brought out around noon, covered by the big moving blanket I bought, and they look cold but not dead yet.
- The interspersed young tomatoes we stuck in the ground under the windows were left uncovered. They didn't make it.
- The winter squash in the southern beds were all covered, but a couple of the little pumpkins without good contact under the plastic got nipped. We'll lose a few there, but the rest looks good.
- The butternut squash weren't covered well enough: we only had two heaters and it's hard to get the air circulating under those tall plantings. Some of the leaves near the ground got frozen, and I'm a bit worried about root damage.

Overall, I think we saved about two thirds of the harvest. Not bad considering. We'll know more when the sun comes up and we can check for soft or discolored roots. (If a squash softens after a freeze, it's no good, unfortunately.)

t:
* The boards and blankets protected the winter squash that were covered. The ones I could see were unscathed; a few that had been left uncovered are a little wilted or shriveled at the tips. Nothing lost yet.
* The kale looks okay (except what was left out of the row cover, which is shot). One of the patches of chard looks singed; the edges are brown but the rest of the leaves are okay. The tomatoes look frostbitten, but still green and perky. I don't expect much fruit from them, but new growth has been coming on late all season, so let's hope. 
* One of the beds with onions had no cover at all, and those were blackened at ground level -- but the scallion tops poking out are still bright green and alive. Not sure what that means for the bulbs.
* The boats protected most everything else, but one of the row covers blew off. Everything under it is a bit wilted, and the tomatoes under there are blackened at the stems but still green.

So far, so good -- nothing lost but the last of the broccoli, which went out last Saturday -- but I expect we'll have more damage by morning as things defrost. If you see anything that looks like it's beyond help, go ahead and pull it now. If it's just frostbite, leave it for now. We'll assess in the morning. The important part is what's protected: the remaining winter squash, the kale and the onion bed. Those should come back.

We'll be out at first light to take stock. If there's anything that looks salvageable, we'll box it up for the pantry tomorrow. If you're able to come help with that, it would be great -- we're going to have A LOT of kale to clean and chop.

If you want to bring something to help us along, come with extra hands or bring coffee. We'll make a pot and keep it going -- and anyone who helps can have a cup. We'll take snacks and pastries too. Gotta keep our energy up.

And thank you, thank you for the coverings and the word -- the row covers and the old bedsheets made all the difference, and several of you took time to come out in the cold with no notice. I know it's an early morning commute for a lot of you. This garden couldn't do what we do without the people who show up when it matters.

More later as we know more

t:
- Squash. Half of them made it. There's still five good zucchinis, two small acorn squashes and one giant specimen that was under a deep cover and stayed above freezing. The leaves on the rest are toasted, and the insides are probably mushy. On the plus side, the good ones look fantastic and we'll get some squash soup out of the not-usable ones.

- Tomatoes. I was afraid they'd been a total loss, but when I picked up the cover on the row that had the three old varieties, they looked okay. Not great, but intact. The forecast was 27 for the lowest spot, which is what we were seeing under the cover. I think those three survived. The rest are in sad shape. Lesson learned: next year I'm putting the tomatoes under the same kind of heavy cover. Maybe even moving them to the cold frame. 

- Kale and chard. Both survived, which is great news. 

- Peas. We left some out and they're toast. We'll see if the ones in the greenhouse overwintered. 

I'll go back down at first light to assess more thoroughly, but it's not looking awesome for the tomatoes we intended for donation. Joanne told me there are some winter tomatoes at the Kirwan's, but nothing on the scale we'd planned to deliver.

On the bright side (sort of), we're all getting a crash course in cold protection, and we'll be way better next year. And we still have some really good squash and all the kale and chard we can use. Everybody is welcome to come help yourselves to anything that's salvageable. I'll put up a sign by the gate with details.

Thanks to everyone who braved the cold with me yesterday. Special shout-out to Marcus for running back and forth bringing more fuel for the heaters, and to Icelandic L conjuring extension cords out of thin air so we could use the 240-volt heater. You all rock.

More updates as we have them. On to next year...

—Karen

t:
• Almost all the kale survived. Maybe we'll have to dump a leg or two onto some of the chard that looks frost bitten, but we will have kale.
• The chard took a hit but several of the smallest leaves are green, and the plants themselves are alive. Likely we'll still be able to pick them, but they won't look as "glowy" as the ones the kids started using in the soup last week.
• Carrots look fine (I said a prayer to St. Rumon, who guards root vegetables).
• The last of the Roma tomatoes made it, every single one, including tiny ones we were going to gift to the first-grade class as "baby tomatoes". I held up a few as examples of how cold it had been when the kids asked why they weren't in their lunch yesterday.
• Zucchini and yellow squash are a sad story; just about blown off, as was most of the butternut squash that wasn't under covers. :(
• There's one last bed of "Hopi Red" that forgivingly didn't frost. Probably enough for a small soup tureen but we'll see what happens as it ripens.

Praise be that we still have kale and tomatoes. The propane worked, and people came out in the cold to try to save the rest. The pantry will get some, and we'll send the rest home with members. But if you see someone crying in the parking lot tomorrow, now you know why.

Prayers to those who lost crops to the October freeze of 2019 and wisdom to those preparing for the one coming in 2020.

(If you're not a member but would like to help with the harvest or donate to St. Brendan's, reply to this thread and I'll DM you about details.)

t:
• Giant pumpkins alive and well – those thick, waxy skins are somewhere between ridiculous and miraculous. I couldn't stop poking them.  
• Delilah's special blue hubbard squash all mummified. We pulled the two biggest out to see if there's anything left inside – didn't look good.  
• Winter squash up in the raised beds (closer to the street) all survived – you can see frost on the leaves, but nothing killed yet. We left a heater at their feet and another under an old sheet over the tomatoes.  
• Tomatoes are a mixed bag: a few of the beefsteaks directly in the path of the creek wind are crispy, but the big heirlooms under the sheet are still warm to the touch. Unclear yet if we'll get any more. Adds insult to injury that we're just starting to see "number 22s" on some of the yellow pears.  
• Kale and chard under the floating row cover are alive, though a little wilted. I peeked under the edge of the sheeting and it's icy down there, so we'll lose some, but not all. Chard is tougher than kale so I'm cautiously hopeful.  


Best case we lose about a third of the harvest – worst case half. Either way it's worse than usual, but better than 2006 when an ice storm flattened the whole south half of the garden. 

Wilma (our head gardener) says we've still got time to salvage what's left. If you'd like to help:   
• Tomorrow evening, around 6 p.m., we're planning one more run to pick any squash we can still use, harvest the tomatoes that look like they'll make it, and collect the kale and chard that survived.  
• If you have extra clean storage boxes or tubs we can fill, bring them tomorrow.  
• Most important: bring sturdy gloves and flashlights, and your stories about stupid weather. This is how we keep each other warm out there.  


Regardless of whether you can help, please remember the St. Brendan's pantry is insane right now, with lines out the door. If you can spare a few minutes and a bag of food when you're out shopping this week, drop it off at their door on Main Street. They're expecting our delivery next Tuesday, but every bit helps.  


— Karen

t:
Many of the beds are rimed – not much can survive that – but the rest of the garden looks OK. The heaters kept a small protected area from freezing, but we had to move them around as beds froze, and most of the crops are still bare to the air. The peppers and hot peppers took a hit: lots were black, but a few leaves look flexible, and there are still green fruits on the vine. I saw at least 20 good-size tomatoes still hanging, snug under their leaves; the kale and most of the Swiss chard survived, looking crisp but not frostbitten; winter squash seems OK except for the rind on the southern-facing hillside that's white with frost; the green beans in the cold-frame look fine and there are still a few peas tangled in their vines.

We'll need to take stock this morning, but more of the fall crop survived than I feared. I'm grateful we're not starting the season from scratch.

We’ll send another update after we assess the damage and salvage whatever we can. If anyone wants to help sort what’s good and bring it to St. Brendan’s on Saturday, please let me know.

t:
* The little cucumbers — well, they're all boned up. 
* The winter squash looks okay as far as I can tell under the covers, although one of the big butternut pumpkins has a big hole in the lower skin from where it touched grass that's now frozen to it, I think.
* The DW ('darkness-wrapper') tomatoes are very sad. One of them looks like the freeze came up from the roots, the tops all turned brown. The others are only partly defoliated.
* The chicken-wire tomato bed is still holding green leaves and un-frosted vines. I think this one survived.
* The kale and chard is... mostly green. A few wilted leaves here and there but not much damage overall.

The row covers worked, at least some of the time. Where they were weighted down they stayed in place and the plants underneath are green, but in a couple places the wind got under them and blew them off. So we'll need to jury-rig some rocks and cinderblocks tonight to hold them down. (If anyone wants to come down and help and get some fresh chard and kale for dinner, we can put the leftovers in the shed and whoever helps can get first dibs.)

The propane heaters are working but we're using them sparingly; they're not really meant for all-night application and I'm worried about setting things on fire with them. (Although that would be better than losing the whole crop, I guess.) For now I've set them up to keep the very most vulnerable beds warmish through the night, and I'll come back in a few hours to see how much propane we've got left. If it's getting low we may have to turn them off.

So I invite any of you who can spare the time to join us for another couple of hours tonight if you're able to. If we can keep the row covers down and circulate the air a little near the plants, we've got a decent chance of saving a lot of the crops. I'll be here at the shed from about 9 pm on and I can bring some fresh coffee. Let me know if you can make it and I'll text you the address if you need it.

And if you can't make it, please don't worry — whatever we lose, we'll make up for it in the spring, and we can always use a few more hands planting. This is farming. There's always something to do and we can't control

t:
• All the tomatoes that were still green last night are still there, no cracks or damage. I'm cautiously hopeful they'll come back around.  
• The kale and spinach actually look better this morning than they did before the freeze; they even perked up during the coldest part of the night, perhaps protected by their leaves frosting over.  
• The chard's leaves are a bit whacked but look like they're reviving. We'll lose some yield but not the whole crop.  
• Squash are almost all done; we lost three butternuts and the one acorn that was still ripening. The rest of the crop was under protection and looks okay.  
• Pepitas (pumpkins) were fine; the flies in the north bed finally killed off or drove off whatever was nibbling the roots, and the vines look healthier now.  
• The arugula and lettuce were not protected well enough in one spot and took a hit; that bed is nearly lost, but we may salvage scattered survivors.  

The propane heaters worked well in the blocks closest to them, definitely made a difference. Everywhere else felt like a freezer. 

We'll know more after today, when we see if the tomatoes and chard recover and how much the kale sets back. I'm amazed at how much difference microclimate and protection made. Thanks again to all who braved the cold and showed up. 

If anyone wants to help identify which of the nostrana seeds sprouted as something else (it's a jungle back there), you're welcome to join me this afternoon. And if you hear anyone asking about free bedsheets, that's probably me. We're down a few now.

Let's keep our fingers crossed and eyes on the south-facing beds today. I'll post photos later if anyone wants to see how row covers look after a night like that.

—Karen

t:
All heat lamps and covers went up just as the sun was setting. We had three big sheets over the tomato frames and the big bed of kale, two for the zucchini beds and one over the winter squash. We couldn't cover the spinach (it's a pain to unroll and roll up because of the Wayfinding Trail running through it), the arugula or the mizuna, or the space we save for the seedlings. 

We had ThermaCare lamb's wool wraps on the pepper plants and wax paper under them to retain moisture in a pinch. We moved all the potted peppers inside the shed and covered the front with one of those thick moving blankets we got from Andy two winters ago.

Most of the crop survived. Only a few tomato plants at the edge of the beds got hit. I found four that were toasted. We'll dig them up and compost them. All the cucumbers that were out feel like they took a bit of a hit — the vines felt crispy and the two on the trellis were a bit brown. That'll probably mean fewer pickles. 

Everything else looks alive and not particularly worse for wear. We'll see this morning if the chard survives — the varieties we're growing don't always handle a freeze, and it was the most vulnerable thing we had out. 

So overall, we dodged a bullet. Thank you all for pulling together on such short notice!

Now we sort through and salvage what's left of the cucumbers (before they get mushy) and pick everything that's roughly harvest-ripe and not damaged — tomatoes, peppers, green beans, winter squash, kale — and get it to St. Brendan's by noon if we can, before Mass. We'll save the root crops (carrots, turnips, beets, sunchokes) for the community Thanksgiving feast on the 21st, and any kale that's left over. And whatever didn't survive goes into the compost.

I'll post another update tonight after we get home from St. Brendan's so Joanne can say thanks if she's around.

 
Walk safely, folks. If you don't feel like braving the cold and spooky darkness on the solo trek down Grammarsville Road tonight, we can use volunteers tomorrow afternoon to harvest anything we missed, and anyone who can help sort or bundle for the food pantry is welcome. Baby sitters for the little ones are always welcome, too.

—Karen

t:
* The coldest bed in the driest corner took a licking. Broccoli is melted, kale is a bit crispy at the edge, all the tomatoes got nipped below the first flowers. 
* The tomatoes in the protected bed under our old blacksheet didn't wilt — the vines at the edges burned a little but the leaves are still firm.  Potatoes were fine under cover.
* Winter squash in the bed that faced north and had two old comforters on it were untouched. Not a frost mark on any of it. In the bed behind it, facing west, about half the vines burned back, and minor frost on the exposed fruit, but nothing killed. 
* Pumpkins in the same bed fared better than the butternut squash did, maybe because of their thicker rinds. The heater sits right behind them and the stems are still green and firm, fruit untouched.
* Spinach and the spring greens didn't make it under their sheet — got crunchy — but the stash we'd already harvested for the pantry last Tuesday and Wednesday is enough for what Joanne wanted.
* Kale survived well enough that I can still grab a big wash of leaves from under the sheet. (Will be lots of coordinated scheduling for kale and cabbage pickup this fall!)
* Minestrone chard is mostly toasted, but again we already have enough at the pantry from last week.
* The greenhouse cucumbers all died once the heater gave up the ghost early this morning, which is a bummer. (I'm working on arranging some winter heat for the greenhouse. Stay tuned.)

No word yet from Marcus on the heater, but he did show me a thermocouple readout when I passed by about 4 AM; the air under the sheet at plant level was holding at a steady 40 degrees, despite the outside temp flirting with 26 at the lowest. 

We'll harvest everything that's salvageable as soon as it thaws out today, bag what we can't use, and drop it off at the pantry after vespers. With the warm spell coming after the freeze, anything we lose now should be more than made up for by the final week of growth. 

If anyone wants to volunteer for extra pantry sorting help after Mass today, please let me know.

For what it's worth, we've got a standing offer from the pantry for donations of any hardy fall cover crops people are willing to plant in the empty beds right now: turnips, kale, spinach, peas, even winter rye

t:
the squash look okay — even the stuff without covers survived. We didn't lose the tomatoes or kale, but the chard took a hit and we lost the late cabbages that were out on the south edge of the perimeter bed. That's disappointing, especially the cabbages. My basil, the purple pepper plant and one of the late cucumber vines that were in unprotected spots didn't make it either.

So we're down on yield, but not down by as much as I expected given how cold it was. No one wants to brag about surviving a freeze, but I'll say it anyway — good job, team. We protected what mattered most. And next year we reinforce the perimeter with cold frames and overwinter a couple of extra beds with tunnels.

Joanne will still need our harvest — the remaining tomatoes and kale, and the squash once it cures a little. We'll have enough for her, just not enough to share with the springhill.coop. Thanks again to everyone who pitched in, and good morning to anyone waking up and wondering how we fared. We're already talking about next year's cold protection plan. Coffee's on.

t:
the kale under the row cover is fine, a bit limp, but green and showing new growth. The kale out is black all the way, even where secured under a big old sheet. (I saw a rabbit exploring along the edge earlier, so I'm guessing we scared a lot of them out of the warm spot.) The chard looks similar to the kale. The one bed of collards not under cover just survived - it's wilted but still showing some green. The tomatoes lost all the still-green fruit. We'll keep the old-growth tomatoes under the cover for now and see if any growth resumes, but there's no color at all yet.

The winter squash and pumpkin are a mixed bag - a few were covered and are intact, but the squash next to them are damaged or killed. It looked like a walking line of frost - the cucumbers went the same way. We have a few good pumpkins we'll keep for seed, but the rest is not harvestable. The little turban squash under cover is ok and will keep growing, but the rest died.

Not what we hoped and not what the pantry needs, but this is gardening in Zone 6B, and we knew the risk when we put the crops out. Thanks to everyone who braved the cold, and especially to Marcus for staying up until 3AM with the heaters and coming back out again this morning already prepping the cold frames for fall planting.

Let's meet tomorrow evening to do a little triage. We'll rescue what we can and figure out our priorities for what we plant next week. In the meantime, I'll ask the pantry if they'd like anything else specific for their free market next week - soup greens, perhaps, or beans?

Be well this week.

—Karen

t:
- Winter squash: the ones under the row covers and bedsheets made it unscathed, but there's some cold damage on the uncovered plants (a few stems blackened, a few of the yellow squash leaves wilted and yellowed). I gathered everything that looks OK and put it under the new暖 chopped straw we made last week, in case temperatures drop again. No losses yet, but we'll have to keep an eye on those spots that got cold.

- Tomatoes: all the varieties under row covers look fine. The beds we sheeted with plastic are good, but the ones with only bedsheets showed some frost on the leaves (which I pruned off). They look OK for now–I'll watch them closely for blossom-end rot, which can happen after a freeze. I pulled a few lower leaves that are limp, and there are some green tomatoes underneath that I’ll check again in a couple of days.

- Kale and chard: some of the kale under row covers is lightly tinged with frost on the lowest leaves, but looks healthy above the frost line. The unwrapped chard showed damage down to the crown on a few leaves—I've cut those away and will watch for any sign of rot on the stems. I think we'll still harvest this week, as long as no more freezes come through.

- New lettuce trays and the microgreens: I brought all the floating row covers forward and tucked them in tightly around the seedlings (we have extra covers from the greenhouse). I put the paraffin lamp I use in the propagation trays out there, but I can't plug it in until we get an extension cord out there safely. Lettuce seedlings are looking fine in the morning; fingers crossed.

- Strawberry beds: the plants that were mulched survived. The ones without enough mulch had some blackening on the crowns—cut away the dead parts and they should regrow as long as the roots are still firm.

All in all, we dodged a bullet. There's going to be some extra work this morning and we may lose a few misshapen pumpkins, but the pantry share is still on. Many thanks to everyone who braved the cold last night, and to Marcus and his father for coming out to help set up the heaters.

Let's keep praying for mild weather over the next few nights. I'll send more photos and details after I finish my rounds.

Stay warm,

Karen

t:
We got lucky with the cabbage and broccoli -- things in the back beds and under the larger row covers only got a freeze, not a hard freeze. That means we should have some cabbage and broccoli for the pantry. The heat was on overnight but we don't yet know whether it worked. The things closest to the heater, like the fall radishes and the broccoli are probably ok, but the cabbage may be frosted around the edges.

In the front beds, the thing that got us were the old bedsheets. They're mostly cotton and let more of the cold through than we realized. We're getting frost burn on the things under the sheets. Specifically a lot of the kales are frosted, the pumpkins now have frost stains on them, and the peppers are the most iffy. The tomatoes actually look ok so far -- we just got lucky there.

The most important thing for now, though, is that our families have vegetables for this weekend. Tonight if there's anyone who can get to the garden to bring the veggies back to the house, that would be ideal. The pantry will have a pickup truck and come down tomorrow morning if nothing else.

I will update on the frost levels tonight. This morning everything just looks frosted more than frozen -- frost damage will be fine for eating, freezing damage will need to be cut away.

Other than that, I want to say thank you to everyone who's helped this year.

With the garden in our second year now, we got six times as much produce into the community as we did last year, and we did it with about half the volunteer hours. This is a big step forward for how much the garden can help in the future. I might actually be able to get back to my research if everything stays this way next summer!

In particular, thank you to our best two helpers, Marcus and Joe, who are responsible for most of that improvement. Thank you to the 15 of us who were able to get out there yesterday to help. Thank you to everyone who's helped out with anything this year. And a special shout-out to the people who spend hours there and I never see -- our volunteers who like to go out there early or late on their own, and the families we empower who use the garden on their own.

I'll keep the Garden Journal going for anyone interested. Thanks for everything, everyone.

t:
Our biggest problem for a warming trend is always the fog, which can fill up the garden before dawn and stay after the sun rises. The fog isn't an issue today, though. The sun is out.

Our heaters, one in each end bed, are running nice and hot. I can feel the difference, even with my cold-weather clothes on. They weren't out when I checked yesterday, but they look great now.

Our only problem is most of the row covers went away. I have no idea what happened, but they're all gone. There are two piles of vegetables in the beds we covered with large sheets, but a lot more are uncovered, and those frost blankets are not going to cut it in 26-degree weather. The first two or three rows I went through looked fine. The tomatoes, beans and kale all look great.

Overall, the plants look like things went well. They're not too bent or twisted, which means they weren't stressed too badly. The kale in particular looks strong, and our greens are our biggest fall category this year. Between the frost blankets and row covers that are gone, I'm guessing we'll find that the rest of the uncovered plants died or froze enough to damage them, but it's a start.

The only question is our squash mat, which the cold hit latest because it was behind the heaters. The top few rows of squash look okay, but the bottom rows look like frost got down in there, and you can't tell for a while if the leaves recovered or if the cold went deep enough to affect the fruit. We probably lost the butternut, but the pumpkins may bounce back. They were only barely ripe anyway.

If we didn't lose a lot, we may still have something for the St. Brendan's food panty. If we did, I hope their vegetable tables were packed the day we were supposed to harvest.

We're all hoping for the best.

(a) It's no longer frozen. The topsoil was wet when I poked it. This is the first good news.

(b) Everything I checked that was under cover, either in the cold frame or wrapped in blankets or plastic, is not wilted and not waiting for euthanasia. The pumpkins looked fine, the green tomatoes were still green, and everything in the cold frame, from celery to kale to chard and lettuces, looks good.

(c) Everything that was uncovered is dead. The broccoli and Brussels sprouts disintegrated into brown goo, the green and yellow beans shriveled to a dark brown. Most of the chard disintegrated as well, but one plant was completely wilted but on the cusp of resurrection.

In other words, this freeze killed everything that wasn't protected. That's how a true freeze works.

So what does it mean?

1) We'll be taking all the green tomatoes back to the kitchen this weekend. I'll give everyone a count of how many pounds it's going to take to make a decent salsa and the order of play to prepare it. We'll use the propane heaters on Sunday to protect the tomatoes we're planning to put back out.

2) All of the vegetables in the cold frame survived, though some of the lettuces may be a little floppy. They'll need a couple of days to unfurl in the sun before we harvest for St. Brendan's. This is promising, because the lettuces are really tender, and it's pretty cold-tolerant if they made it. Plan on spending the work day with them.

3) We'll see about the covered chards and kales. They're not frozen now, so maybe we can bring them back, too.

4) It was an operational success.

Bottom line: We can fend off light frosts with covers, but for a full freeze, now that winter is here, we're going to need to get even more serious about warming the rows. The good news is that several garden members--maybe you--have heaters we could use to keep the beds warm.

At our December potluck, we'll make a plan for warming the beds in the winter. We'll also be talking about replacing some of our soils with soil that's more sustainable in the long term, and about what to plant for spring.

t:
- We didn't lose a thing in the back beds (as of yet, anyway.). Yay to heaters! The tomatoes are looking a little worse for wear, though, and we know now that a lot of them gave it up.

- Everything in the front beds (where we couldn't set up heaters) is solidly frozen, though. This includes our chard and kale, and most of our still-green tomatoes. The tomatoes, peppers, kale and chard that were wrapped in row covers or blankets survived, though. In the front, we had three beds covered in row cover, and all the blankets that I could beg friends for. Though the tomatoes in the back beds get sun all day, and the front beds got none today, they were still protected.

- All the squash and pumpkins look good from what I can see. There's no worse than a slight limp on the vines in the front beds, and I think many of them lost their blooms. I'll know for sure in a few days, and we should see real signs in the next few days like the pumpkin vines turning brown.
- All the herbs look ok, with the exception being oregano and basil. The oregano is limp, but not dead, and the basil is...we think dead.

- What we lost last night are the three vines each of pumpkins and squash in the front beds, the kale and chard in the front beds, and the peppers in the front beds. We also lost anything small in the front beds that wasn't wrapped.

What that means for our fall harvest is still up in the air. I'll follow up about that tomorrow. :)

A huge thank you to everyone who pitched in. It was a team effort, and I'm so glad we all pulled through.

One last thought...we need to learn how to better protect the garden during the winter from our erratic weather. I'll ask the master gardeners at our Jan. 15 work day for some input, but I'm wondering if anyone has any ideas on the discussion page?

Some frost on the squash leaves left out in the open in front of the back beds, but they're still ok. One pumpkin has a white end that a neighbor warned me about, but the rest is fine. The row covers look great. All the lettuce appears untouched. All the turnips seem fine. All the cilantro, dill and parsley all look fine. Everything in the back greenhouse seems fine. It was 26 on the heater on one side and 29 on the other.

The issue is the three covered tables out front with 150 pounds of tomatoes, squash, eggplants and peppers. They got bad frost. The biggest crop of peppers ever and most of the eggplants. Almost all the tomato crop as well.

We also lost about 200 pounds of kale, chard and lettuce in the unheated greenhouse behind the trailer. It's a bummer, but the good news is now we have plenty of garden space to plant more chard for our next donation in 6-8 weeks. That way we can help people who need it now and also fill the shelves again in winter.

So, that's the damage. The majority of our fall/winter greens, all the squash, most of the tomatoes and eggplants and 90% of the peppers. It just goes to show how much one good rain three weeks ago can save. But we also got some rain yesterday evening combined with the warmth of the covered containers. So that may have made a difference.

Thanks again to everyone who came out. We'll need to replant now. We can always use hard labor. If you haven't seen the garden I'll bet you wouldn't believe all we've done this year with a crew when we were bored and some light labor when we weren't, all against the almost certain march of gentrification. We're not done yet.

So I’ve been a member of this community garden for about a month now. Overall I am pleased. I’ve been sharing a plot with the developer of the garden and was given lots of advice and support. The developers were key, but I feel that the community is as well. We all share responsibilities of weeding and watering “our” community plots. No one seems high strung or power hungry. A community garden is by nature a shared space and most everyone understands that. We don’t allow alcohol or children. Everyone does their part and feels pretty good about what we’re doing.

If you’re considering joining a community garden, here are some things to think about.

Check out the site: Is it a feasible distance from your home? Who else is gardening there? How many plots are there? Are only certain crops permitted? What’s the cost? What are your responsibilities? How can you get in touch with the owners and/or members? Do not take over a plot that isn’t yours or another members. Before you start planting call to talk and see what is already growing there-you can always check out the plot as we did. Share your knowledge -gardening is a great way to find friends, but no bragging about your garden to those less experienced. Gardening involves a lot of labor, and no one needs to feel slighted. Especially if you’ve been slacking or are beginner.

t:
We lost all our tomatoes. All dead, frozen right down. They took down the last of our peppers, too. There's nothing to eat, and we may have damaged the plants enough that we won't get anything next week. Our summer squash and most of the green beans are toast. All our ground basil was killed too.

We saved lots of stuff. The green chard seems fine. The rainbow chard suffered some burn and maybe will recover. All our kale is fine. All the fall herbs survived. A lot of our winter squash, while a bit burned, might still mature. We'll know in a few days. The winter squashes in the back beds are a total loss. Everything inside the greenhouses that was covered is fine and nothing inside those structures was damaged at all. There was zero frost inside the greenhouses, so there's definitely options there. The asparagus in the front polygon is all fine. There were no casualties among the plants inside cages, and that includes the broccoli, cauliflower and collards.

In short I'd call 1/3 of last night's harvest a loss, though it's possible some of the other squash will still make it. Our first frost date is technically November 16 and we're always a bit anxious the 2-3 days before that. Last year's early frost cost us much of our brassicas (kale, collards, etc.) but we didn't have greenhouses then. This year we made it to the frost day but didn't get past.

With the temperatures staying in the high 20's tonight the unripened squash are pretty much toast, and we're going to have some definite casualties on Tuesday. All our peppers are gone. That's likely from last night. If Tuesday does what it's supposed to do then the damage will be extensive. After Tuesday we're likely safe and it'll be swing back to normal for a bit. So I'm trying to make sure we've cleared off all the peppers and all the green tomatoes for today. There's still a fair amount of ripe squash that will need picking from the back beds, and the pepper plants still have a lot of peppers that will need saving. t:
99% of the stuff covered made it—including the eggplant that Marcus started from seed. Thanks, Marcus! Even most of the stuff left uncovered but well insulated by the beds made it. We did lose a few tomatoes, the beets, and... most of the winter squash. Winter squash is one of those cold-weather crops that people plant late, so they can wait until after the first big freeze to harvest. But we didn't know about these until we bought the farm, and they were still on the vine last night when we put the covers out. There might be a small handful of pumpkins we can save but most of the butternut, acorn, and spaghetti squash won't make it.

There was a little frost on one of the kale leaf tips, but that was it—every thing else looks good!

I will let you know closer to the weekend when we're taking donations to the pantry. I'm going to try to hold off until we think we'll have more squash than we can handle, but I don't want to push it any further than we have to.

In other good news that we found this morning, the back beds are now full of rotting leaves. I guess Marcus and I bagged up the mulch to make sure ours was super well insulated this week, so I want to get out there with shovels and toss some of that over the fence if you don't mind.

t:
The two heaters definitely did the trick. As far as I can tell, nothing in the back beds suffered any damage, and there was almost no frost on any plant tops. The squash and tomatoes behind them had at least six inches of snow on top of them, so I don't know whether the frost got them.

The four boxwood shrubs we got from the county in May have brown leaves and dead branches, which is a shame because I have been watching them all year from the bed and parenting them like a baby.

The kale and chard had beds with heavy frost, but the row covers were over them and I could feel heat radiating from inside them. This morning they are wilted but much less frost-damaged than you might expect, and I think they'll thaw out okay.

The front tomato plants under the row covers and next to the heaters fared the best. The far north corner rows that were not protected yet at all look dismal (which does not surprise me), but the veggies we picked for St. Brendan's look fine. I can't get them to Joanne today, but she wants them on Thursday with the rest of the veggies we harvested earlier this week, so that leaves us a day to make it happen. But there are no signs of any frost damage on them at the moment, so we should be okay.

This is the same story with the remaining pumpkins, butternut squash and eggplants. Some of their leaves have wilted from snow, but their tops are all intact--at least so far. The big pumpkins in the back are still growing, although they have been exposed to the cold every night for the past week.

The cold also did a number on my back--I'm so sore I can barely move today. I went to bed and had some ibuprofen for the pain. All my joints hurt, but I think they'll be fine.

The good news is that tomorrow is 50 degrees, with a high of 61 on Wednesday and 66 on Thursday, so our veggie rescue is definitely back on. With it being so warm, all our crops should thaw out within twelve hours. Our primary worry is fungus. But we won't have to worry about harvesting anything that looks weird or yucky--it'll all go right to the compost pile.

t:
The weather service was off by one degree, and we had a confirmed low of 25.7. All the squash is still on the vine, looking sad and a little wilted but still alive.
All the kales and chards are down. All the tomatoes look bad.

As far as the rest goes, the heaters kept the heat up overnight in the beds where we planted the $60 worth of seedlings this fall. Their rowcovers look great, all snuggly on the rowcovers racks, and all the greens are still there.

This isn't over. We didn't know if the heaters or the rowcovers would work, and I don't think we're out of the woods entirely.

I'll walk through in an hour to check on things, and we've got volunteers coming in this morning and this afternoon to do some replacement planting because all the covered kale got frozen too.

Still, we're cautiously celebrating. Tomatoes and the hard squash are a toss-up at this point, but we did lose most of that. On the other hand there's at least one or two surviving kale plants in all but two of the raised beds and the big ground bed, and most of those we planted this fall still look good. If everything goes right for the next three weeks we still have a harvest to look forward to by the start of November (though it will be a lot less than we'd planned on).

This didn't happen just because the weather service was wrong; everyone who came out worked and worked, getting that kale, kohlrabi and Swiss chard down, with bean trellises that were still standing so solidly three months later it took three person-hours just to take them down and get those raised beds ready for the freeze.

We don't know the final score yet, but we're so glad to see a good fight.
