t:
We've been lucky so far. Most of the ground is still unfrozen, and the forecast says it won't get below 30 again until December. Saturday morning it's supposed to be 43.

Nothing in the tunnel got damaged overnight. Some of the hoops got a little flat, the corners in particular.

All the melons and winter squash are fine. Although some of the big pumpkins appear to be in the movie Twister, with their vines wrapped around them. The green tomatoes are still setting, and there's another big pineapple tomato about to turn red.

All the peppers are green, as are the jalapenos. I was really hoping to get to the orange stage. Some of the tomato plants look a little unhappy, which shouldn't be too surprising.

The big beds where the heaters were set up seem to have come out okay. We may harvest a little kale this weekend (after it warms up enough), but we'll still need to let the chard keep going for another week or so. The squash seem to have grown some, and we may get a few more blossoms out of it this next week.

Everything else in that bed survived, so that's excellent. We were most worried about the kale in bed three.

Bed three, column one, that's the kale bed. The cold air down-flowed from East Main Street, with the broken orange hoop and the bedsheets covering the plants farthest up. There's not a lot of forage there -- I think the cold just laid them flat instead of killing the plants.

We'll pull the cover off in the morning and give those plants a good blast with the hose -- that should flush out any lingering coldness. If it doesn't work, we have another hoop to replace the flat one; we'll just put it a couple of feet further back.

Bed three, column two: everything looks fine, except for the squash in the front. I might pull the squash and transplant something else in its place; I'm not sure we'll get much fruit out of that squash.

Bed three column three: everything looks fine, except for the two pumpkins right behind the tomatoes. The leaves still look green; hopefully if we cover them overnight tonight, with an electric heater in place of the propane, we'll get some serious pumpkin color.

Karen

*   **Kale and Chard:** These are surprisingly tough! Some frost on the leaves, but a lot of green still survived. 
*   **Heaters:** Marcus and a few others braved the cold keeping the heaters fueled, and they worked. The beds with the heaters are in much better shape than the others – mostly the herbs and some of the peppers.

last night was a cold windy rain, with very little ice anywhere. There's some damage to the fruits of our growing season: a couple of eggplant in the front bed, but no squash. The peas and beans are dead, which is okay because they had already had their day, but the tomatoes and kale and chard will be a disaster. Based on what I remember from hurricanes, the lowest parts of the beds will be even worse when the water runs off during the day and crashes into the cold earth, so one more reason we're all grateful to Masduka for the raised beds.

The rain continued tonight and is still going hard, with steadily decreasing temperatures. As of this writing, the weather widget on my computer says it's 31 degrees. I am heartily regretting the fact that we had to take the heaters down last night - both because it's dark and both because the hard freeze is over. They weren't gasoline backpacks, just plain old patio heaters. But now the temperatures aren't the problem. They're below freezing, yes, but there's still no threat of low temperatures anytime soon. The problem is the water. Wind-whipped rain, soaking everything down to the earth,  wicking heat away, both before first light and again as day breaks. Daybreak will probably be bad - when the cold air hits directly rather than moving overhead through the air, it will probably kill everything. As a rule we'd hope for commensurately bright sunshine after that, or the ice slicked plants would be dead - but today and tomorrow are predicted to be gloomy with overcast skies. Bottom line止损方式:. we'll know the extent of the damage in the morning, but we are likely to have a disaster on our hands.

So what do you do with 30-40 pounds or more of vegetables that are in varying states of mushy, snowy ice? Maybe a few of the tomatoes can be used, if we work fast this afternoon to cut injured fruit out of the plants and are really careful to pick up only the partial tomatoes that appear to be hard and flour rather than frozen mush, to help them keep their shape. Then we dry them as quickly as possible to remove as much exterior water as can be gotten out, before a very hard freeze sets in. Then cover them over and see what we can salvage in the morning. Or maybe not. They may all be ruined.

Squash is such a delicate fruit

Tomatoes are toast. Damn, we don't even know what line we have, didn't have a chance to taste them. We harvested about two dozen before the freeze, which I'm taking to St. Brendan's at a couple of hours. Melons are frozen solid. Got some pictures coming later, that's just crazy. Beans were shredded and then killed, no more flowering and only half a dozen podlings got picked. But Cinder's Korean black is producing even after tomato size green beans and looks like it will carry it through to frost. Other fall greens are intact. Too dark to read the temperature strips, but I did a taste test: greens are too cold to eat but not necesarily frozen, but the tomatoes are definitely frozen.

We did the best we could, but even a couple of hours difference in temperature knock everything, so the survival rate is maybe 40% for the commonly cultivated crops. Night before last it was about 36, with most of the green tomatoes still on the vine, now they're all frozen, but it will still mend an oven roasting job like this. Maybe this is just the head of long hard winter, but I'm not looking forward, and it's only November.

Tomorrow will be warm and sunny, so we'll harvest the frozen veggies and throw everything else back out to try to nurse them through to the sheaves.

If there's anyone interested in getting a share of the frozen tomatoes to the parish community table or worse case cannning, let me know. Thanks for your prayers,

good gardening.

By the way, I tell you this because it's not warmth that freezes plants, it's how fast it gets cold. F0 has a killing temperature of 28, and we have a hard freeze warning several times a year, but not really harm. Sudden drop from 70+ to 32 is deadly for some hardy plants, like tomatoes and melons. On Monday it was 70 with a few fog rolls until 8pm, drizzle until midnight, then a front blew in and it started off clear and calm at 23 and got colder and windier all night... very fast downward cross. I read somewhere online that they could vacuum plants for five minutes before the freeze and they woiuld be OK, but we don't have that kind of thing here. t:
in the area that was well covered, there's only a small amount of damage to the tomatoes. I would be out picking as usual but the row covers and sheets are still frozen nearly solid.

The squash and pumpkin all survived. The resilient Delicata stood up particularly well. (They're little, squat, antique pumpkins with orange and brown stripes; Delicata means "little delicacies" in Italian.)

All along the edges, especially on the east side where the slope drops away, everything was choked by frost. You can see it glowing in the flashlight's light. The kale and chard were pancaked flat. The lettuce and endive were too tender even for a row cover, but they've made it through most of the summer and brought some good leaves to the kitchen. It's no big deal. A few tender tomatoes were piling up in the cribbage leaves there; they all fell over, and I heard a loud crash and had to jump back.

Marcus's artichokes along the block edge are frozen, but they're annual anyway so he'll harvest and set aside the root to overwinter and replant next year. The Purple Casper carrots in that bed were looking good.

The early plants that are going to seed froze solid. I can see seed heads on Red Vale beans and Italian Globe artichokes hanging like stickers in the cornfield.

The herbs, which we usually use medicinal and only had out for fancy coffee shop type embellishments, are dead or dying. Rue and Rosemary have the best of it. The nettles along the block edge are as black as they are in any freeze, but they revive in late winter. I'm not sure I'll be taking money for them until they recover.

All in all I think we lucked out. We have a decent fall crop to bring to St. Brendan's, some jam and squash to preserve before the days get too short to work much out here, and what to do in winter but a dinner menu, preserves, and a stack of blankets to sew with the raspberry triples. Here's to the hardy Delicata and the tender hearts of the Garden Club of Arkansas!

BuiltWith Moz: The Intersection of Bio-Technology and Integrated Architectural Design

Emma Crevling, a University of Washington student, presented her thesis project, entitled "Builtwithmoz.com", at the Design Studies Graduate Program Thesis Day on March 15th, 2011. Below is her accompanying research/thesis statement:

My research in the field of architectural technology comes from a letter received in the mail some years ago from a prisoner sent from the Brazilian rainforest to her lawyer. The letter describes a glowing water source that kept hundreds of prisoners alive for six weeks in pitch dark, awaiting rescue - and the spellbinding photos taken by the lawyer at this unbelievable discovery. Evolutionary evidence in ancient rock art spanning back over thousands of years to extant photography attests to the ongoing symbiotic relationship between our species and these organisms. Phosphate. Carbon, energy. Sentient, bioluminescent, oxygen producing algae; the prehistoric, microscopic balancing agents of our holobiontic existence.

A “living building” with heat, electricity, and waste management systems growing autonomously on site; beyond greener architecture is functionally alive in its constitution like a once extinct greenhouse experiment, but better, through exponentially biological sophistication. Disequilibrium is central to this concept. Thermodynamic poisons from hydrocarbons are absorbed and filter fumes from a polluted city in an urban residence 2030. Exotic aliphatic aldehydes are newly evolving, instrumental parts of a symbiotic environmental system. Photobioreactor systems are then stabilized, encapsulated, freeze-dried, or cultured - waiting to populate. Harvesting carbon from the atmosphere, supplying essential amino acids and vitamins, releasing high amounts of oxygen, algae-out eats algae-in at year’s end. Bio fuels are now carbon neutral or better. Property that is no longer through intrinsically biological biddable course. Auxin, a deal killer, is optional, bio-fuel optional, glow optional, the scope is open and variable, a biologically based agenda explores multiple possibilities.

the squash is mostly pien, so that bit is gonzo. Two pumpkins were obviously done by morning already. In addition to the pumpkins, we've lost two Obladi Oblada sunburst, two butterfly, and one Kabocha and one Dumpling squatz. Two oblanas are gonzo too (I can only guess what grape is left under the heaped soil). Some of the surviving oblanas and squash were damaged; on close inspection of a Kabocha there are small patches of clear ice.

The tomatoes are gonzo; all the fruit is white and frostbitten; not even human chickens find those edible. The largest ones we'll give to the chickens (and we still have the tomatillos and blueberries to feed them. We still have edible tomatoes left in the greenhouse though, less than a week older than the ones out here. We're all just kind of sad about the tomatoes. We spent a lot of time with them.

The greens are mostly OK. The loose row covers we had piled over the beds froze into the soil in a fluff of angry ice spikes. In addition to raising temperatures under there they added weight, and nothing got bruised. The bell peppers were also covered, and also mostly OK.

The rest of the squash are still alive. Those big ol' flat oblanas will provide some great meals. We were also sad to lose the blue potatoes. Those went down fast. I'd guess most of the firekeepers melted the potatoes on the way home.

The worst thing I can tell us right now is that the intensive beds are gonzo, the cover generally didn't reach the soil under those. It was simply too much space and not enough cover. The plants are flooded with ice and the soil underneath will take many days to thaw; most if not all of the information is lost. On the coldframes we lifted the clear covers without incident. The vegetables inside are OK.

I have to assume the whole garden and yard are now favors-only, please no pets, kthx. It'll be harder to wash off than the rad sludge after a months-long flood, but there's ice all over, and you don't want that on your paws.

So remember to bring gloves every week though November, the soil stays cold, and we're not using so much hot compost anymore. Also remember to keep clearing short paths through the garden to the back beds, the pumpkins are blocking them.

t:
the tomatoes all look pretty good--there are about 15 plants, each with fifty or so red and green tomatoes. No damage so far, and they seemed really low to the ground, which should protect them. The kale, chard and other greens look great, including the purple kale with its pretty purple-red color. They're also close to the ground and insulated well.

Many of the squash, melons and cucumbers were really damaged, but fortunately most of the squash had finished ripening and we picked most of them yesterday--hurriedly, I might add. It's the squash still ripening on the vine that looks bad right now.

The bad news is that we'll get those freezing temps for two more nights. The good news is that Gouin tells us the vegetables could probably take that. He says it's the leaves above the veggies that protect them and the fruit is right next to the warm ground. So if we keep the leaves protected, they can handle a brief freeze (and row covers and sheets help) as long as the sun comes out the next morning and warms everything up. That's why the forecast for continuous cold now through next Monday is worrisome.

The book "Month by Month Gardening in the Carolinas" says, "If a light freeze (29 to 32 F) is in the forecast, surprising solutions include covering plants with pine straw, dry leaves, sheets, or boxes. Let the covers stay on until midmorning, well after the sun has risen andarming your garden. The most drastic and extraordinary yet effective measure is to wrap your plant in two layers of foam insulation. Lay the insulation flat on the ground, cut an incision up the length of the insulation, and slide it around your plant." Our recommendation is to use fabric row covers or sheets. Once you get to this stage, it's time to sit back and wait, but if necessary, we'll start coming down every morning, wrapping them in something warm and coming back in the afternoon to check.

Some good news: no signs of fungus yet. I've made seven gallons of 0.5% purpuridin, a homemade fungicide. So if there's any sign of fungus, we'll hit it.

Our beds furthest from the creek survived the freeze better. Joanne suggested we replant all of the badly damaged beds in March. It's still too early to replant, so let's all just watch, protect, and wait until March.

t:
outside row cover, the lettuce is dead and the kale is severely damaged. Our older plants are about black and gone, but we have a few dozen tiny winter seedlings we're going to nurse through the winter inside the greenhouse, and we still have a few hundred lettuce seeds. The last time our lettuce crop died was spring of '08. Come spring of '09, we'll have seedlings to share.

The squash under row covers on the beds were all frosted hard last night. They won't be usable even as organic material, so will have to get chucked. The potatoes are all row covered, and as long as everything clears between 26 and 32, we'll be fine. We'll be looking for new sources of sweet potatoes, winter squash and cabbage, and need to find more space for potatoes in spring.

Probably the hardest part is going to be keeping a collective and individual focus through the setback. After being scalded by the summer drought, many of us came out swinging early to get everything in. We know what can come with crop loss: worry, sleepless nights, lack of appetite. As long as we have that focus, we know how to get back.

I want to encourage you to stay positive. Acknowledge the losses; there's no way not to-- just don't let them take over. The coming months are a time for talking and eating, for going around the garden daydreaming with seed catalogs in hand, kitchen timers in our pockets, scheming and dreaming. We are so self-reliant in most of our habits, and especially here. We know only love feeds us, plants and humans both, and draw our strength from that. Keep talking, come to the potlucks, sit on the steering committee, share seeds and cuttings, donations and startup costs for big projects.

Things were bonkers at the garden yesterday, and awfully quiet this morning. I want you to know we are fine. We knew we were pushing the dice on these late crops. We're a young garden, not fully immune to setbacks. We're not set up now so that mistakes like these won't still happen from time to time. Hantha just buried his most serious setback of the year; he isn't too traumatized just yet, but it could happen over the winter. That's why you see us not only diversifying our plantings, but diversifying the steps we need along the way; why we're casting all the spells we can think of

The tomatoes look like they've had it, not a surprise since they're our latest crop. The kale and chard seem fine. The squash is a different story--they're frozen solid. The huge sweet dumpling we were really looking forward to turns out to be badly rotten, big chunk of it cut out already by mangled vines. Rain must have started to freeze come up through the vine to rot it. I didn't check them all, but long islanders look like they fared better; sharon and kobocha may have survived to be donated, though they're cold now. The peppers and eggplant are nothing.

Marcus came down an hour ago and the squash all still needed lots of the frost combed off leaves and vines and off the squash themselves. Nothing terribly efficient or practical about trying to harvest that way, but Marcus did it anyway. I'm so grateful for our team. The grower at the back beds called out, "Have a good day, Karen," as I left. I was down there so late that the diner across Sungod had already closed (bonding with the cooks at Olive Garden All Night Diner is also part of being an Eastgate grower!)

Tomorrow decisions will be made--do we withhold everything from the pantry but the donated kale and chard? Short term, that could be lots of hungry families, but the pantry has plans for their gardens next year and a small hoop house. We may miss this year but get more lasting impact with a good harvest next year.

We'll be talking about the garden tomorrow, too, at a community meeting in Washington Park. Come to join in on what would be a good dinner if enough of us are there!!

t:
• Except for some tomato plants near the pathway, the tomatoes are untouched. Yay!
  • The Halloween Jack squash and yellow Delicata squash are fine. Yay! 
  • The pumpkins did get a little chill, but are going to be just fine. Yay!
  • The cucumber was killed. Ouch.
  • The tomatillos are dead, too. Sad.
  • Everything in raised beds on the shady eastside is dead. The kale, the chard, the Swiss chard, the cilantro, the lone basil, the parsley, even the old cucumber vines...  everything is dead. That's not so bad, considering what it was intended for--but I hated seeing that basil go. 
  • The biggest pity is broccoli. We've had such a long run of our lovely in-spring broccoli, and now it's gone on the same winter morning my spring collards showed up.

Is that it? I gotta say, that is better than I expected. I expected the broccoli to be fried enough that it wouldn't come back in spring, and for the kale and chard to be dead. Well, that's not how it went.

Now let's look forward and plan for next season.

This garden came as it was--a flat piece of ground next to a creek with no direct sun past 1pm right now--and it's been a fine little spot, but I think we need to do something different in the future. Half a garden plot is a long way from a raised bed because, being so long, the extended mass of earth holds heat even when the tops are under snow. That's enough to allow our brassicas to over-winter and start early in the spring. When they're protected from frost by a snow blanket, they usually survive just fine with cover or mulch over the root crowns. That part is all good.

But the other half of garden plots are seemingly there just to be half, and filled so haphazardly that they're just puddles of garden soil that freezes solid in a week of frost. When the frost comes again, the fertile beds become small ponds that drown plants--even under complete cover. This half of our garden plot, on the east side, is useless.

t:
definitely cold enough to kill our squash, cucumbers, beans and tomatoes. Those that weren't already dead were down to a trickle of leaves and vines.

Luckily, we planted winter squash with the intention of having them that way, over winter. Both winter and field squash are cold hardy enough to leave them out if temperatures are consistently below 50, and once night gets down to the freezing point you know they're going to stay there for a while. You might lose a little on the frosty nights, but the squash is down to the pulp at this point and will perk right back up by spring.

Basically remember this: when frozen way down, tomatoes go mushy and squash just get a bit more hardened off.

So, I checked the winter squash, and yeah, they are definitely frost-kissed, although the low temp let up a little and more vine was alive in the morning sun. If it gets below 26 I would move them under the row cover we used on the tomatoes and into the compost area. Like we did last year, you can bury them up to the fruit and then the cold soil will keep them a little longer.

So, all in all, we lost our first tomatoes and some other stuff, but through the secret ancient act of burying crops, our winter harvest is safe. Yay!

Lesson learned:

t:
there were some heavy frosts in the neighborhood, and the grass, strawberry leaves and basil all showing obvious damage. The winter squash say its temperatures just fell from the 30s. The rowcovers were pooled with water 1/2 inch deep, and peeking through the rowcovers I could see lots of dew on the skin of our squash. So either they were cushioned enough from damaging temperatures, or some heat was radiating from the soil below high enough to support the temperature inside the covers.

However, farther down the beds, where the covers weren't as tightly drawn or water wasn't pooled inside, the temperature was about 32. That's made up partly of the relatively warm air trapped inside the cover, but probably partly the cold air (and maybe some ice) outside. The kale was tightly compressed by our winter rowcover, and was about 36 in the middle part of the row. t:
Winter squash: It's toast. Sizes of many, many winter squash only a hair shorter than the average pumpkin, every squash frosted and slumped. Even the ones under row covers are a bit slumped. Now I know why people rush to dash their squash and pumpkins.  The squash bugs finally, finally went away a few days ago -- what happens when whole bedfuls of klingons all die at once? The decaying tails of a large snippet on the back fencing adds one of the creepiest sci-fi accents you've ever seen. The neighborhood critters who finally ran out of squash bugs to eat are now surrounded by essentially dead squash plants too.

I picked all the winter squash I could. Some were ready anyway, some are probably done now. It's hard to tell by flashlight, though, and I didn't want to disturb them.

Tomatoes: I covered everything as best I could and put all the lemons and limes in trash bags last night. This morning, I can't tell there was a freeze at all. They withstood it perfectly. We'll have a nice chance today to figure out where the well-draining spots for next year are, now that they need hills of dirt.

Everything else: Watered down as it was by the light dusting of snow we got, it was still bitterly frigid. The cold would have come up through the ground, and left things easier. It would have left the vines across from the pathway to the garden just beyond bad. I could grab a kale plant in the front and pull it up just a quarter inch.

That's good because there were a few dark spots on them.

Although the tomatoes survived I could also see frost wounds on a lot of their leaves. Again, that is really odd, because frost usually spots out the lower leaves first, plain and simple kill of the distant new growth, and generally go against gravity.

Frost bite: I've never seen this happen in the rather extensive organic gardens I've made a habit of managing. Frosts almost always follow a generally predictable pattern: Everything with any exposure first, then the unprotected and downwind positions on frost free spots, proceeding up the hillside and leaving sun-warmed walls and outcroppings safe. This pattern has often been perfect, even down to the very edge in almost every case. Which is why I set up windbreaks in the first place. 

    I know planting choice played a big part here: The garden is literally a snowdrift farm

The root cellar is not insulating (it's temporary) and the night was very still. The temperature should have dropped at least 45 in there. I'm pretty sure the squash is put. (Frost can get inside when the coldest air in the morning is sinking down through roof vents.) The benefit of diversity: some seeds got an early, expensive lesson in hardiness, and may pay off in medals next year when a mom knows what will be reliable around here.

One of the back tomato beds is clear. The French Scablast was MAYBE 45 if that big squash protected it. The red currant cage was as warm as the tomatoes, with more overall foliage cover. If there's still healthy green leaf, it MAY be OK. If the canopy of leaves protected the ripening fruit may still be OK.

The front tomato bed shows leaves hit by 41 to 36. On the major favorites like TheToeIndia, about 90 percent of the branches in the worst spots last night fruited. Maybe TTI's readiness is like an airplane engine ... it can lose a lot and still function. We have an extensive TTI seed supply from customers with whom it's become a heritage, hardy enough to survive in their unique microclimates. That's the biology we have to work with.

TEMPERATURE IS THE only accurate predictor. Is temp 38 in your cold zone? Check for green on the MIDDLE span of a leaf. If there's green, look at the stems nearest the lowest leaf clusters. Look at those branches very, very carefully for green mesophyll. If there's even the greenest tinge, that branch is most likely not cold-damaged. Some red or purplish veins may be 35 or 34. Green is 36 or warmer, no other valuable crops get that bitter. See PPrunella and pha cloudDuster for more details. If something is protected by the leaf pile or stacked closely to other plants that have no green fingers left, it MAY still be ok. Look for green. Anything that didn't make freezer O'Shap or Italian Swiss recipe has to be left and still protected during the daily cycle, but it gets very painful quickly.

Orv's tomatoes are red, but not purple. If a real hard freeze comes, Orv was not cold-damaged in UK-18, either, so we will go on together with that highly productive breeding standard.

The damage is likely still spreading. The more that it's covered, the more warmth can remain in the soil, the more roots can continue their work, and the more the plants can continue to grow.

everything that we covered is fine. We'll get a decent harvest from the greenhouses. The cover crops look great. The kale, chard and collards we didn't have time to cover are all down to the ground where they're covered by the foliage of surrounding plants, and so we're hoping some of them survived well enough to regrow (and freeze survival rate is a big honking question mark). The tomatoes have (literally) ice scattered across the rows, so a large bite of our harvest is probably gone. They can often withstand a little frost but this looks like a very deep freeze and we expect a lot of damage.

The most significant bit of damage is inside the fence but around the outside perimeter...where we typically keep storage boxes, mulch bags, garden hardware, tools, and so on in the fall. One of those items is our wood-fired oven. Yesterday under freeze conditions the temperature inside the oven was a toasty 80 degrees. No smoke alarm in a garden, and little risk of a blaze, so there's been no rules about getting those grills out in the middle of the night. And of course, overnight we all iced in for 7 hours when the temperature should have been down below freezing.

This morning I walked through the garden with iced-over flannel dangling from my arms in the growing light and smiled. I think the survivors will be OK, no one's hurt (that we're aware of), the garden's going to come back, nothing really big got destroyed. It's a very weird feeling, especially so very early in the morning.

I'll update you more tomorrow as we pull the covers and do our own assessment.

The red ones seem to be doing okay, so we'll have a bunch of canned tomatoes if we can still process them. The chard and kale are in good shape, except the ones that were a little smaller and didn't get row cover, those are cold but not frozen. Same with the peas and some green beans. The carrots, radishes, lettuce, cilantro and spinach are looking like they got their last dinner, the string beans the next day or two. I say that just to say if you táke them it might make someone else happy because I took them.

As for the squash and pumpkins:
The spaghetti squash are in great shape.
The pumkins are a little warm to the touch, but look like they need a week or so more, so they're still a little green. They will all be fine after a couple days inside.
There's a heap of butternut squash are totally frozen, which you can't tell from the outside, but they're close and they're chopped open, and they are frozen solid.
The white pumpkins are fine.
The black F1 and Blue Hopis are fine, those being under the row covers are great.

We had been harvesting in small batches, so there will be a lot more tomatoes, kale and chard to harvest. Marcus was going to let the ones under the plastic sit for a day so they thaw totally, and then we should be able to harvest as usual, so more of that to come. Same for the mums, which were just starting to open out. And the pumpkins will keep.

That said, we'll be talking about putting in a permanent heat system on the back beds probably with some outdoor, thermostatically-controlled, electric-controlled heat mats. Monitor the temperature, and know when to turn it on so you can take the out of that zone. The beds we put the heaters close to seemed to have stayed in the 50s to 60s, which is why the tomatoes seemed like they made it. With some help and some luck we've salvaged more than we lost, so that's where we stand, and we talk about next steps Friday.

t:
The squash and tomatoes supported by cages were close to ground level, and froze solid overnight. (The temperature never reached 32, but the length of time near that mark was lethal.) Every single flower and every new bud on the tomatoes froze. Our hardy (we thought!) tomatillos also died. The green (literal green, not ripening) peppers up top of the plants are fine.

The miraculous thing is, most of the rest of it survived. The grapevines and the tomatoes supported by the trellis survived. The tall Swiss chard, presumably because its cold air was above its top leaves, is still standing. The brassicas, roses and lavender survived.

I need to list why this is such a jumbo oversight on our part. A hard freeze is a matter of the temperature reaching 32 for long enough to damage plant growth (usually just the buds and leaves).

The roses and lavender, as most of you know, are very hardy plants that naturally survive long freezes without protection. Their buds bloom in early spring. Roses do in fact die back in cold weather - but that's a normal part of their growth cycle. Mulching a rosebed will get the base of the rose through (relatively) unharmed, and help the root system keep its strength. Once the roots get their summertime, wintered roses almost always revitalize themselves. Lavender, not so much: frozen lavender doesn't go dormant - it can get leaf spots, die back or just die.

The brassicas, as I said, are hard to the point of annoyance to kill. If we get the weather the forecast is predicting, our kale harvest will be over in a couple days - but a lot of what's left will keep going into the winter, and we can expect some of it to regrow.

If our squash had been left out they would frozen and soften and get mushy very quickly - but actually, maybe we did them a favor by halting their growth. Many of them were still green, and the next step for the squash is to lose water and get firm. They need to dry and let go of their sugars, so preserving them with age doesn't mean we lost them forever. This is the first we've tried to force-harvest, and who knows, it might be a better way.

Most of the fruit-and-herb terraces seem to be fine. They're hardier than the annuals - the actual frost is lovely in flowers, but very bad

t:
we lost a half dozen tomatoes, some colder where they were touching the soil and some where the leaves got wet with night condensation (a hazard of the row covers). Most are OK, although of course they're a little slower to ripen now that we're seeing frosts.

The duskier squash, like the orange and greens, were damaged badly. We will still have the yellows to harvest, and we have a fine haul under cover in the milk crates on the shelves.

The lettuce is looking really good under the cover, green and fresh as icebergs.

The kale and chard sustained some freeze burn, but should still be edible. The arugula is looking a little shaken (see photo).

Our vining squash plants are stone dead, roots into the soil. The fruits will still be fine, once we get them picked up from the foliage.

This frost may have cut our harvest by half, and our timing is even worse now that tomatoes ripen more slowly at night freezes. But we will have a harvest. And we learned a lot.

A few thoughts about how to make row covers work for you at home:

1. Row covers are best if they don't touch the plants. They keep air under them warm and still, and the plants themselves get the benefit. Most of our tomato damage came from cold hitting the lower foliage and from plants that touched the cover, like arugula. Lettuce is fine, under cover, because it's a more tender plant. Anchoring with blocks on the sides keeps the fabric still without crushing plants.

If you don't have extra row covers and don't want to rush out and buy them (quite expensive), try bed sheets. We've had good luck with those. Old curtains work too. Meantime I will work on getting more row cover on hand for next season.

2. Young plants need more protection. They're small and tender. The oldest tomatoes seem to have had the best luck. Grown-up tomato plants may get a little freeze burn and some bruise and blackening along the leaves, but they recover and start making fruit again. Seedlings? Not so much.

3. It's hard to protect low-lying beds if water and cold air keep pouring down over them. Next year we need to rethink the garden design to account for elevation concerns of all kinds. Topography matters.

Freeze Alert - Let's protect the plants! (update)

As some of you may be aware, there is a hard freeze warning for some parts of Columbus on Wednesday night/Thursday morning, with temps expected to dip to, and probably slightly below, freezing. The garden, due to its location by the river, has dropped to below freezing on a number of occasions this fall.

We propose to try to protect the tomatoes, beets, kale, chard, broccoli, and other plants that could give us at least marginal crops. We've planned on using the row cover fabric and the propane tank heaters we bought last year. I am counting on some of you experienced winter protectors with bring sheets and tarps with you to cover any vulnerable crops. Items from your gardens may be moved (provided the plants will still fit; the back beds are very crowded) into the two communal beds beside the arbor and covered.

The propane tanks allow us to light two heater lamps. To do this safely, any propane tank being burned on site must be monitored constantly for the duration of its burn time (about six hours each).

If you want to help, please sign up using Doodle. (editor's note: See link in the Eastgate Community Garden members group on NextDoor if this post is in reply to an earlier message.) Last year we had about ten of us from 7:30 to 9:3

t:
everything that was under the covers survived. The tomatoes, squash, kale, chard, broccoli, sweet potatoes, tubers, and basil were all fine, and the lengthening days mean they could still produce for the food pantry. The space I worked on was over 25 degrees, and the difference as I walked from covered to uncovered beds was the difference between spring and winter.

But two beds lengthwise in the center of the garden were mostly open. Our row covers didn't have enough room to go around the length, and it's the one side of the horticulture coop that doesn't have its window or door, so the wind hit it hard. Everything that stayed uncovered is crouch-down-on-your-knees-dead. Third of our beds was unprotected, and that third of the garden is a total loss for the season.

The things we took cover off of this morning are all warm and full of life, and they've already started growing again. The uncovered beds needed to come down, and that'll give us time to get in spring crops. But this is a heartbreaker. Garden memberships are the only revenue source we have this fall, and right now our chickens are late on feed, the chickens we lost went unfilled for our spring chicken share, and we need materials and tools to rebuild the coop, hatch chicks and get the hives ready for the winter. This was top of the bill this fall, and now it looks like we might lose a quarter of our membership funding.

We're still standing, but this one hit us hard.

Still, this bed has some basil and some broccoli that will still come in, these seedlings we transplanted out in rows should be strong enough in two weeks to cover parts of a bed each, and the tomatoes and squash are still out there. We're going to laugh at that weather on the other side of this one.

I'll be back in a couple of hours with my flashlight, to see what else came through. If you know folks in the West Branch community, maybe pass this message along: the fall harvest is important to the garden, incredibly important to the families we work with, and after next week, we'll be giving away everything we have left to our neighbors.

t:
Sweet Corn #1 Surprise, Little Thumb, Sun Gold, and the two grape tomato varieties went out. The large heirlooms survived. There were no serious surprises. The winter squash were on the edge; I saw one yellow crookneck, one zucchini, and a derby that may just eke out an edible interior. The cucumber concentrate, which is close enough to be mirrors of each other, were all fine. Joanne told me she'd love to get our cucumbers, so that's good. Everything else mostly survived, even the peppers. So much of what we grew isn't supposed to be out when it goes below freezing, so we've been cultivating our defenses for months. The main loss of crop came with the tomatoes, which we'll make up for in the spring, and a lot of the winter squash wasn't mature enough anyway, and probably would have burned its net caloric output in curing and storage. What is lost was hard on our gardeners' hearts, but not in the quantity of food we'd expected to give away.

Though our defenses are strong this year, that's not always the case. Last year we staffed up way into November, trying desperately to get ready for the first hard freeze, but then it froze everything for the next month. Two years ago single freeze destroyed the whole tomatoes, including variety I'd been saving seed from for three years. That happens when the last of the tomatoes turns color all at once, just as hard frost descends. I just dealt, but not everyone wants to deal with that possibility. When you're the person who volunteers to save seed, or commit to a crop, or spend months starting something in early spring, and the freeze gets it, you either hear advice on weather, get a course in how to defend crops better, or have a cup of tea by the Agora fire and feel bad. The Agora is open to gardeners, if the latter option sounds more comfortable.

So there were no surprises, and that's a huge bonus because the garden is such a good learning context, even when things go badly. Every significant loss a garden has had a silver lining, whether that was the mass-canning project of '15, the collaborative work that sprang up last year, or the high-quality seed we've been saving over the past three years. t:
first, the good news, the heaters kept the temperature in the covered beds above freezing until just before dawn. At about 7 AM the temperature was 31-34 under the heaters and in the beds covered with 2 heavy layers of row cover. All the squash and potatoes planted there were fine, and the tomatoes are OK.

All the pumpkins in the front beds did freeze, though. There were 3 rows of pumpkin vines along the fenceline, and almost all of them are toast. I didn't cover them because I thought they were mature and hardy enough. Apparently not.

Fortunately those were the remaining yellow interpretations of zucchini, not the Munsters we mainly collect for the pantry. There are a couple of partially rotten spots on some of the Munsters, so they obviously got too cold, but I don't think they're bad enough to lose entirely.

All the winter squash I tagged earlier are fine, they're not yet ripe enough to finish their color and it's just hardening the skin. The wind snapped off the green brackets from about 1/3 of them. That's OK, they'll ripen a little more slowly.

Most of the kale and chard was covered and is fine, but the uncovered plants that were against the fence are pretty much lost. The tomatoes against the fence are toast, but the ones in the middle of the beds are still out there.

3-4 of us are heading back down in the next hour to remove the covers from the winter squash and mature tomatoes and carry the heaters and propane tanks out. We can at least try for the tomatoes in the covered beds if we get another week of warm weather.

Next season we're going to need way more row cover to put over the tomatoes when winter squash don't need it. We also need to get the tomato plants a lot higher above the ground, they need the heat of the soil, and the leaves need to do a better job of protecting the fruit as they set. We're also going to have to do a better job of actually planning next season; we put too much of our best plants right next to the fence because there wasn't enough room wherever we thought they'd go. Just plain lack of forethought.

This worked out OK, although the pumpkins will be a big loss. We have some winter squash, kale and chard coming in, which is what we really needed for the food pantry, so the tomatoes and tomatillos are a plus.

t:
damage to the Roma tomatoes was about moderate. Most were still upright so I was able to carefully pick them. On the trusses that hit the ground they were shredded and mushy, or even withered into brown globs. We'll do one more round this morning before final cleanup.

The winter squash appears to be OK. No soft spots, no shriveling. It will have to prove itself as storage quality but I'm cautiously optimistic. The kale is toast, and the chard dehydrated. Everything else looks fine. There's celery and arugula and garlic, plus we have beds of potatoes we'll dig another day. It doesn't look like we'll fall short.

Help me shout out BIG thanks to Marcus, Brian Mulenga, Dahley Mobley, R.J. Schultz, Linda Jacobson, Amber Torres, Liz Westfall, and whoever from the Occupy encampment was on the toes. We owe them all a cheeseburger. Some of them were standing in the garden in the morning cold, wrapping bananas and green tomatoes with newspaper, to try to keep them a few days longer.

Today's to-do: Rebuild the root cellar on the hoof. Find packing materials. Sort, scrub and store the squash in cool, dry locations. Move quills into the greenhouse. We'll get the pickup scheduled and look for someone to drive. It hurts us to see the effort of dozens of people and millions of bees whose lives revolved around making this food, and not get it to the community it was grown for.

This system is fragile. If we caught two torrid autumns in a row, food security would be in bad shape here. I think we made a good harvest and saved what we could. We owe the folks at St. Brendan's more than we can.

But we got something, which is more than we could've asked for in other years. The dry, cold winter we're in now is conspiring to put us in strong shape for spring.

To the eternal struggle of the farmers. I hope the rest of you all have good food in the cold days to come.

t:

Only a couple around the edges were wilty, so we won't get all of our squash, but we'll get most of it: tons of kabocha, butternut, Delaware, white delight, and long green spinnies. The vines are all dead.

Tomatoes: For the most part the same thing. We have a barbecue grill on wheels, so I put some of the old newspaper under the grill, put the grill over the tomatoes, and covered the whole thing in a row cover and an old sheet and cornered it like a tent. All but the ones right on the edge under that were fine today. The others not so much, but we should still get hundreds or thousands of red and green tomatoes, and a host of figs and bloods, too.

Just a little of the chard blackened and can be trimmed off. A couple of kale plants, the salad mix, the peppers, the parsley were already in their bales of straw, and they all made it. Well, except for the peppers and two huge eggplants, which we were really hoping to squeeze through the night. We tried to give them a make-shift little greenhouse but it burned down!

t:
The survivors
The row covers on the open beds worked, and most of the tomatoes still look okay. Some of the very young tomatoes were damaged, and maybe some of the larger once, but we still have quite a few hearty, violet-tinged, orange core cherokee purple tomatoes that won't have any internal discoloration. They're less delicate and freeze better than normal tomatoes, so as long as they're not heavily bruised, they'll still be okay to harvest and freeze. Wheee!

We also had an old bedsheet protected FRONT ROW of tomatoes, where we always plant Sun Gold tomatoes. That row was completely protected and is chock full of beautiful Sun Gold cherry tomatoes. These tomatoes also have some frost damage, but they're mostly fine.

We also covered our winter squash. I'm not sure yet how they fared, but at first glance they all appear to have survived.

The losses
About half the kale was cooked by the freeze, but I'm buoyed in this loss by the many many hardy plants that are now sown. Those will (I assume) grow well in early spring, when we really need them. I know charcoal leaves on twisted stalks are not what anyone expects for their kale, but I think they'll recover (if we don't lose the beds to the weeds, which we're not totally managing). Our biggest loss will probably be about half of our chard.

Thoughts on the future
This is, I expect, the future for how we garden, no? We're always going to have unpredictable frosts, but I find it hard to imagine we're not going to start getting our fall frosts earlier and earlier. As I have said, our *spring* planting season has been extended by 1-2 months over the last 14 years, but the opposite seems to be happening on the other end of the summer. How are we going to grow tomatoes in the early spring, and still get a harvest before fall starts? This was a productive year (in addition to the ones for which I still haven't posted entries) but it took a lot of accommodation along the way. Velma

t:
the squash was the most vulnerable, because we didn't know which had already made the sugar switch that keeps it from freezing. Even the natives would have suffered, and definitely would have lost the babies. That means no spaghetti, delicata, buttercups, clock, long bananas, yellow heirloom or intricate nabecorn squash, and most of the pumpkins. We could probably still make pancakes out of the intensely tiny little ones, and might have jerky from the butternut, since jerky takes serious freezer action. The flowers on the poor man's watermelon were probably killed, and the inside may be damaged, but we'll have to wait and see. The heat-loving beans would have perished, too. They won't recover from caving to freezing this week, though they could grow back behind the frost, so everything looks dead now. We don't know what the chili peppers will do. They're bred to thrive in freezing climates, but not just after they've been shocked by the cold. They pulled back almost all their leaves, but probably already stored most of their sugar, so we'll have to wait and see on those, too.

Some others were fine. The arugula and lettuce still look good, as expected; unlike their summer counterparts, they're meant to withstand this sort of weather. So are the radishes. Things to watch are the tomatoes and greens, particularly the kale. The tomatoes' leaves all folded up, but didn't look like they suffered ice damage. This may not be apparent until it thaws a bit. The fragile curly kale had some setbacks, but the regular sort and the chard seem okay. Things to re-cover/fold up and warm tonight are the broccoli and cabbage, and the cool-weather chives and pansies.

So in summary, we're sitting a little lower on squash than we were last week, but are still expected to have a good fall harvest if the weather holds. We anticipate having both tomatoes and greens through the early part of next year, and after a good frost the arugula is slated to launch into overdrive! It only needs to come firmly above freezing through this next cold period; if we do lose these beds to the snap, any overwintered stock (lettuce, radish, kale, chard, even the cilantro) can take over next spring.

t:
Tomatoes: probably a 70-80% loss. The plants themselves are mostly fine (you need more like the mid-30's to freeze tomato plant tops), but almost all of the tomatoes turned up withicles.

Most of the peppers are fine. The mature eggplants browned, but the smaller ones seem OK. I think we'll get some of them before the big frost that's expected Sunday night/Monday morning.

The kale, chard and potatoes seem to be fine. Some of the squash turned into cubesicles, but most are fine. We're losing some of our diversity for sure, but I don't think it's as bad as I feared.

There are some great lessons here for our first year. First - 2 inches of mulch is almost useless against frost, but 4 inches is really helpful. Second - row cover is great for young plants, but once they get up off the ground they're more susceptible to cold at night. Next year we want to weld chicken wire into a covered system. Third - strawberries can be easily protected with a hoop-and-row-cover system, but we probably want to aim to have the bulk of our crop by early October.

Encouragingly, we only lost one of our needs-as-tomatoes potatoes!

So that's where we're at. Report back if your garden fared better than ours, please.

Thank you SO much to everyone who came out to help. If you're interested in signing up for more alerts (especially for Saturday afternoon working days) please go to eastgatecommunitygarden.org and sign up on the form.

t:
the squash leaves (which are usually sitting flat on the ground with just the unripe fruit peeking out beneath) are still able to ripple in the wind, whereas last night they went flat as if they'd been set in concrete. So the actual leaves are dead. The fruit looks like it still needs a few more days to ripen (you can't even squeeze the skin anymore), but if we've been able to protect the vines without squashing them out there's a better chance the fruit will ripen. We're still at 32 in the temperature pocket where it is, so we're not done yet tonight. The heaters are still running, and the blankets are still all over the place, and the sun isn't due up for five minutes yet.

The kale and chard (some of you remember two summers ago when Robert planted hundreds of plants to help save the local between-season school lunches) are so mottled with freeze damage that we'll have to pick them and see what we can salvage from the centers. Same for tomatoes. We'll only know for sure if the leaves perk up at all by the end of the day, but right now it looks like at least half of the plants. They'll probably be able to sprout again if the ones we pick don't all end up shriveled, but that's too late to be useful for feeding kids at school.

Will fetch my camera and take some pictures and put them up after the next round of sunup freezing.

So bottom line: these heaters and blankets have been training wheels. The plants were not ready to be on their own. We are now staring at a huge shortfall in vegetables for the pantry and for the school. If we don't have a consistent chain of warm weather in the next few weeks, this is another year where we'll have to look for donations from grocery stores or farmers' markets. Our pantry coordinator graciously tells me they will take whatever we can give, and some of you have donated in the past, just let us know if you can contribute look through the produce drawer in your fridge. Even a little of what we planned to give will be welcome.

Thanks for all your hard work so far, and if you can help in any other way, please still do.

the kale is just fine. It looks like the new, tender little plants we put out yesterday for next year's harvest will be fine.

The tomatoes also seem okay. Most of the fruit had already turned from green to red. The rest remained green but so do some tomatoes left alone during short frosts here, so we'll wait a while for the true signal. All of them will be immediately ripe now since the cold nights affect ripening hormones, so we'll likely be running a big harvest this weekend.

The squash looks mixed. There are some white spots on many skins, but it's too early to tell whether they'll be hard and dry or tender and squashy. Like the tomatoes, they likely won't be affected enough to use the same way we would one that's fresh from picking, so we'll need to cook them and can in the next few days.

I wish I had more good news--I know how tightly stretched our food pantry donations are every year and how many families who depend on them don't get many fresh vegetables this time of year. We will certainly send them plenty of canned and frozen crops, but it won't be the same. My real hope is that we'll be able to send Wes two 5-gallon buckets full of great stuff. I also hope that early October freeze we dodged at the beginning of the season helps us catch up a little for the end. That orange stuff getting thick on the clover and pigweed was gorgeous in the flashlight.

t:
the fall kale and chard are fine, and so is the endive. But most, everything else, is toast. The row covers helped a little, leaving a core in the middle and roots unharmed. But they're not going to step back up to maturity from time of year and you just can't reliably grow fruit on tomato and pepper plants this time of year.

So the bottom line is: about 90 percent of our fall planting is dead. The endive and chard will probably finish just enough to harvest a once-a-week bunch, but that's it.

So thanks to all of you who helped. But now the question is: any tips on how to salvage what's left and replace the rest of it?

For those of you unfamiliar with a freeze:

If you've never experienced a weather-related freeze -- which everyone will experience in specific crops sooner or later, despite the nicest forecasts -- what happened is this: cold air is actually heavier than the air around it, so in this case it settled out of the clouds, troughed into the center of Indianapolis, and then followed the path of the White River down into our garden. It's as if the outside parts of the garden got visited by the bad elf on Black Friday.

As the invisible flow of air descended on the garden plants, the cold reached into their cells like a giant icepick and crystallized their membranes -- there you see the evidence in the visible ice crystals that formed, making it look as if the leaves are dusted in snow and ice, though they were perfectly clear when they froze, of course. When the frozen leaves rallied in the rising sun, their prep had been compromised so it began to look as though they were melting, as if a giant iron were beginning to burn them out. But that's because each cell wall had already failed and none of the cells could function to deliver nutrients to the plants, so all of them literally began wilting on the vine.

Now that the sun has risen fully and warmed things, as you can see, just about all of the once-bright greens are now turned into a million tiny skeletons of frost-burned plant flesh.

This is the time of year when the ground is finally warm enough for any seeds that land on it to germinate -- or for hills of fall garlic to sprout under the right cover -- but not warm enough, or with enough daylight, to bring adult-flower plants to fruit.
